This research focuses on resolving inconsistencies in data tables that contain missing values and functional relationships between attributes. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on consistent data tables with optional attributes, our study addresses the more prevalent scenario where consistent tables with missing values and inherent relationships are deemed preferable. We establish a preference-based notion of better-defined tables, enabling us to define a partial order of evaluation. This order utilizes join-like operations that combine tables in accordance with their relationships, taking into account possible missing values. In addition, we identify a minimal table that serves as a baseline for comparison. To this end, we introduce a concept of strong connectedness, characterizing connected tables that can be fully connected without introducing additional missing values. We also explore various types of connected tables, establishing their relationship and demonstrating how they can be converted to each other. To manage discrepancies, we propose a framework consisting of three levels of intervention: eliminating inconsistencies, refining relationships, and enhancing data. This framework is underpinned by the partial order of evaluation, enabling us to determine the efficacy of different approaches. We conclude by outlining possible applications and forecasting future research directions. Moreover, we provide a characterizable class of tables that cannot be fully defined, along with a protocol for validating the superiority of a given table. This protocol utilizes a conceptual representation of tables that incorporates the concept of strong connectedness. We also explore this concept in the context of recursive relationships and tables with multiple levels of attributes. Furthermore, we demonstrate how to determine the completeness of a table with reference to a given set of attributes, along with a characterization of attributes that define a table. We end by examining the relationship between the preference-based notion of better-defined tables and the existing concept of "good enough" tables, along with a characterization of tables that are deemed "good enough" according to this standard. This study presents a novel dynamic model called Temporal-Varying Poisson Autoregression (TVPAR) to accurately represent and forecast time-series data exhibiting significant changes over time, particularly in cases where data counts vary significantly in response to different time periods. Unlike existing models that assume data correlations remain stable or switch instantly, the TVPAR model leverages distributional changes over time to predict its variables. We have developed an efficient numerical method to estimate the TVPAR model parameters and established theoretical guarantees for these estimates. Furthermore, we have established that the TVPAR model can yield consistent predictions, and these results have been validated through simulated examples and real-world data analysis. Specifically, we applied the TVPAR model to forecast enrollment rates and showed its superior performance compared to rival models, as well as the importance of considering temporal variations in its estimation. The TVPAR model has been implemented in the R package tvpar. The code for the model's derivative analysis is available at https://github.com/abdo22/TVPAR. The TVPAR model has been published in the journal Statistics and Computing, volume 33. We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that combines the benefits of neural networks and descriptor fields to facilitate efficient and robust manipulation tasks. We envision NDFs as part of a three-component framework consisting of feature extraction, representation generation, and matching modules. To ensure the representation is invariant to rotations, translations, and scaling, we employ a distinct network that directly aggregates the relevant symmetries, effectively treating the object's pose as a continuous parameter. We then utilize this representation in a contrastive learning-based matching module, where the object is distinguished from a set of distractors. To validate NDFs, we implemented a pick-and-place task using a real robot and found that networks with a relatively simple structure can efficiently determine the poses of objects compared to a comparable learning-based approach. We also analyzed the effects of different network architectures and showed that NDFs can successfully generalize to novel objects by simply retraining the representation generation module. All the code and models are available online at the following link: https://sites.google.com/view/neuraldescriptorfields.

In statistics and machine learning, it is frequently essential to establish whether a particular optimization procedure for a given function can be trusted to locate the function's minimum. To achieve this, researchers often rely on the Mean-Field Approximation (MFA) and the TAP (Thatcher-Anderson-Pearce) free energy method. However, the validity of these approaches near an optimal solution is not universally guaranteed and can depend on the specific properties of the distribution from which the statistics are drawn. This paper provides two key results. First, it is shown that a certain property is shared by Gaussian random vectors, which is not a general property of all random vectors. Specifically, it can be demonstrated that the TAP free energy is a concave function of the optimal solution for Gaussian random vectors, whereas this property does not extend to non-Gaussian vectors. In contrast, it has been previously established that the TAP free energy is locally concave for certain classes of discrete random vectors. Building on this result, the paper also shows that the expected TAP free energy exceeds the actual log-likelihood by a specific margin for Gaussian random vectors, which is a statement that can be verified through direct computation. Furthermore, this result has implications for the validity of the Mean-Field Approximation and the TAP free energy method in the local regime, specifically that the expected TAP free energy and the mean-field log-likelihood differ by a quantity that is bounded by a constant times the square of the distance between the optimal solution and the true parameter. Finally, the paper also provides a novel proof of the local concavity of the TAP free energy for Gaussian random vectors, which is a result that has been previously established but was previously proven in a different way. The paper ends by highlighting an important issue that remains unresolved, specifically that the paper's results do not extend to non-Gaussian random vectors beyond the discrete case. The paper also outlines a hypothetical approach for overcoming this difficulty. Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct tasks: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We integrated projection grouping and correspondence learning models using a fully supervised learning framework, where the resulting predictions enhance the accuracy of object pose estimation. Experimental results validate the proposed technique's effectiveness, demonstrating performance enhancements over state-of-the-art methods across multiple datasets. The code is available at: https://github.com/lingyu2016/DeepHMap++.url}{https://github.com/lingyu2016/DeepHMap++}.

Generalized Graphical Lasso, a method for inferring nodal connections in multi-layered networks, has been extensively utilized in various applications. However, the availability of Python libraries specifically designed for Generalized Graphical Lasso computation has been limited until the development of GGLasso. This package extends the functionality of Lasso, Scikit-learn, and SciPy by integrating an array-based Generalized Graphical Lasso solver, thereby providing users with multiple resolution optimization techniques and direct reconstruction of partial correlation matrices. GGLasso also supports multi-threading for enhanced computation efficiency. Although Generalized Graphical Lasso models can be estimated using R's glasso function, the implementation in GGLasso allows for the separation of regularization parameters for each network, the reconstruction of partial correlation matrices, and network reconstruction based on log-likelihood maximization, all through Python. This library is particularly suitable for various research domains including neuroscience, genetics, and finance. Despite its focus on Generalized Graphical Lasso, the package can be used as a basic framework for solving other regularized optimization problems, as demonstrated by the inclusion of an solver for the Regularized Generalized Linear Model. This package provides documentation, example applications, and user guidelines to facilitate network reconstruction using Python. The underlying code is transparent, with the solver's algorithm detailed in the documentation, along with guidance on implementing custom optimization algorithms. The package is designed to be highly extensible, with opportunities for developing new algorithms based on the existing framework. The community is invited to contribute to the development of GGLasso. The package is available under the BSD License, considered permissive. The version of GGLasso available currently is version 1.0. Numerous biological simulations rely on detailed models of molecular configurations, yet the computational cost of determining all relevant configurations through dynamical simulations can be prohibitive. In this work, we explore methods for controlling the spatial dispersion of configurations sampled using Langevin Dynamics, a popular stochastic integrator, in the context of biomolecular simulations. By analyzing theoretical predictions, we verify that a recently introduced weighted average method effectively influences the configuration sample space. Building on this result, we develop a targeted strategy to limit the sampling to a specific sub-space of possible configurations by adjusting the mass matrix and modifying the Langevin integral, including a detailed derivation of the desired form of these parameters. We further propose a straightforward, mass-matrix-based approach to restrict the sampling to a specified sub-space. The efficacy of these methods is demonstrated through simulations of a simple polymer and the full biomolecular protein GB1, using the AMBER force field, in multiple configuration scenarios. Our results show that both weighted average and mass-matrix-based methods produce independent, uniformly distributed configuration samples that can be combined to cover the entire sample space, thus enabling the simulation of complex systems within a reasonable time frame. In particular, we find that the mass-matrix-based approach offers greater precision in predicting distribution characteristics. Finally, we apply these methods to investigate conformational flexibility in a real biological protein, the adhesion molecule CD44, for which the three-domain structure has been hypothesized but not directly observed, and compare the results with available experimental data. In this case, analyzing the distribution of spatial distances between atoms using our controlled sampling framework reveals specific dissociation angles between domain branches, as well as detailed information about the hydrodynamic helices that comprise the long extracellular domain. In addition, we determine the total conformational flexibility of the protein, quantifying the average angle $\theta$ between helical branches, and find that it is directly related to the charged residue distribution along the chain. In particular, we believe that determining the distribution of specific atomic distances could aid in force field refinement, while further developing these methods will be essential for simulating complex systems that involve the dynamic binding of multiple molecules. This study investigates how spheres interact with running water by being flushed with water at various velocities.  When water velocity is slow, research has shown that a standing wave forms over the sphere's surface, while increasing velocity creates a ring of air that seals the water from entering the sphere's surface.  As velocity continues to increase, the ring of air breaks and water begins entering the sphere's surface through a circular path.  Another air pocket forms in the center of the sphere, surrounded by a rotating liquid pocket.  Ultimately, this inner air pocket is dislodged, and a solid water mass fills the sphere.  Factors such as surface tension and sphere size affect the speed at which water enters the sphere, but it does not depend on the water's velocity.  Rather, it relies on the balance between the sphere's surface curvature and the ring of air and it can be achieved at any water velocity. Humans naturally generate rich auditory feedback while interacting with their environment, which enhances learning and teaching through observation. Despite the prevalence of audio data in robot learning systems, developing techniques to effectively incorporate this data for teaching other humans remains a challenge. Our research focuses on teaching a robot manipulation policy to human instructors using auditory feedback from previous experiences. To achieve this, we employed a teaching system that incorporates a suite of techniques to accurately direct a robot using auditory feedback, accounting for limitations in data quality and uncertainty. To evaluate and refine our approach, we conducted a series of manipulation tasks with a human instructor providing feedback to a robot learning through trial and error. Our results show that the system successfully learned a policy that enabled a 60% reduction in error and a 25% decrease in the number of attempts needed to complete a task compared to using a random policy. Furthermore, we found that the system's performance improved as it gained more experience and better understood the relationship between actions and their effects. Our approach and findings contribute to the development of a robust teaching system that can adapt to various scenarios and scenarios with incomplete data, paving the way for its use in a range of applications including, but not limited to, training human operators for robotic assembly tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/RobotLearning/AudioTeaching.

Conversational interfaces such as robots and voice-based systems like Amazon Alexa and Google Assistant are becoming increasingly popular, and as a result, testing these systems has become a pressing issue that needs urgent attention. Currently, validating these interfaces is a time-consuming and laborious process that involves manual methods and takes a great deal of time and effort. To address this challenge, we present a innovative approach to testing conversational interfaces using a automated testing framework that enables the efficient creation of tests in an efficient and expedient manner. This framework is composed of a straightforward scripting language, a rich library of predefined features, and a user-friendly interface for executing and managing tests. We demonstrate the capabilities of this system through a real-world example, and show that it offers significant advantages over the manual methods currently in use. In addition to its practical uses, this system is also suitable for educational purposes, offering students a hands-on opportunity to learn about the intricacies of conversational systems and the testing process. The system is available for download on GitHub, and we invite users to try it out and provide feedback. In the course of developing this system, we encountered several difficulties, and are confident that other researchers working in this area will also benefit from our experiences. In the final section of this paper, we outline some possible directions for enhancing the system, and offer it as a proposition for other researchers to build upon. The system we developed is suited to testing voice-based systems, but it would be possible to adapt it for use with other types of conversational interfaces. The challenge of validating conversational systems is ongoing, and we are certain that other innovative solutions are also being developed, some of which may offer even better approaches to testing these systems. Single-target and dual-target scenarios are common paradigms used in cross-domain recommendation. In the single-target setting, recommendations are made for one user with multiple preferences across different domains, whereas in the dual-target setting, recommendations are made for both a user and an item across different domains. However, both of these approaches have their own limitations, thus we are proposing a novel MSDCR framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Cooperative Recommendation. This framework aims to enhance the effectiveness of cross-domain recommendation by focusing on a dual-target scenario where recommendations are made for both a user and an item with multiple preferences across different domains. Unlike existing approaches, the MSDCR framework leverages the concept of a comprehensive attribute preference by integrating explicit preference information and interactive behavior. This integration enables a seamless exploration of user preference distributions across different domains. Furthermore, the MSDCR framework incorporates sparse domains that contribute significantly to the recommendation task as ``premium'' domains and adapts a multi-objective optimization approach to enhance recommendation effectiveness. Experimental evaluations conducted on real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of the MSDCR framework along with an analytical comparison to establish the computational efficiency of the framework. The code for the MSDCR framework is publicly available, and it has been successfully deployed in a leading e-commerce platform. The underlying concept of comprehensive attribute preference has been applied in various cross-domain scenarios, thus providing a valuable research contribution. Conic programs are effective for solving a broad range of optimization problems, and their potential is significantly enhanced when utilized within a two-step resolution process. However, natural conic expressions can hinder the performance of conic solvers by causing them to devote unnecessary time resolving the conic representation. We introduce Hypatia, a tool that automatically determines the conic expressions necessary for a precise solution and feeds them directly to a conic solver. We demonstrate Hypatia's capabilities and showcase its potential for improving the efficiency of conic solvers in resolving specific blocks of variables within a two-step resolution process. We also explore a representation that includes natural conic expressions and validate Hypatia on standard test problems, finding it to be a competent and versatile option for conic solvers. The code for Hypatia is publicly accessible. We utilize Hypatia to improve the efficiency of APOPT, a solver for large-scale optimization problems involving the water cycle, and successfully apply it to a real-world scenario involving demand planning. We make the code for this model publicly available. The name Hypatia is given to the tool as a tribute to the ancient library that housed the works of Diophantus, and it is developed under the Hypatia.jl Julia package. The escalating quantity of MRI data necessitates automated quality assessment to ensure rapid and dependable analysis, without diverting valuable resources to incorrect or poorly trained models. In this study, MRI data from six different scanners was evaluated to determine the underlying factors influencing classification performance. A hybrid approach was tested, combining a CNN-based classification model with statistical features derived from image characteristics, scan parameters and temporal variations. The evaluation utilized a multi-factorial design, analyzing the interaction of several factors on performance, and revealed that combining specific scan parameters as input features improves classification performance. Furthermore, this study demonstrated that quality assessment models can be trained to generalize across various scanners, depending on measurement conditions and image acquisition protocols. The results have implications for designing more efficient and efficient MRI quality assurance systems, and highlight the significance of proper training and validation in MRI analysis applications. The proposed methodology provides a framework for evaluating and optimizing such systems. The MRI data and analysis code used in this study are available online. The integration of electric vehicles is becoming increasingly common and significant. This report examines the impact of privately owned electric cars on a power grid's resilience. We developed a decision-making framework that prioritizes grid resilience by scheduling electric vehicle charging, while considering various factors including financing, supply chains, and environmental concerns. We introduced a new objective that enhances grid resilience and implemented a novel charging strategy to address issues of platooning and battery depletion. Furthermore, we incorporated a risk-aware strategy into the optimization process. Our study utilized a real-world case study in a specific geographical region. We analyzed the effects of different scenarios on a test network and found that charging electric vehicles during periods of high renewable energy generation can significantly reduce strain on the grid. Moreover, we discovered that a risk-averse approach to charging can greatly increase the cost of electric vehicles. Our research indicated that a 10% increase in grid resilience would require an additional $120 per month from each electric vehicle owner. Lastly, we concluded that private electric cars have a limited impact on the grid compared to other variables, and that a 5% drop in renewable energy generation could increase the cost of charging private electric vehicles by approximately $30 per month. Our findings suggested that a $5000 premium for risk-averse electric vehicles could result in a 5% reduction in non-renewable energy generation, which would further reduce the cost of charging by approximately $25 per month. Our research discovered that the optimal charging duration for private electric cars was between 9 and 11 hours. Lastly, our study found that a 5% reduction in non-renewable energy generation, a $5000 premium for risk-averse electric vehicles, and a $120 additional monthly fee from electric vehicle owners could reduce battery depletion to 20% or less. Our developed model was compared to two existing optimization methods and was found to be more effective in reducing battery depletion, decreasing grid strain, and increasing grid resilience. Our research provided a theoretical framework that can be applied to other optimization problems involving multi-agent optimization, as well as providing a practical solution for electric vehicle manufacturers, power companies, and renewable energy generators. Our research opened the door for exploring other variables that affect the grid and provided a platform for analyzing the impact of platooning on the grid through simulation tools. Our developed model was suitable for large-scale optimization problems and could be implemented using a range of optimization algorithms. The outcome can be manipulated by agents changing their motivations, but this is counterproductive in the long run. We studied all possible crystal structure configurations for these compounds, and our results show that both GdSn3 and CmSn3 adopt the AuCu3 structure with a very slight displacement of atoms in the alloy. Our calculations indicate that the magnetic moment per cation is lowest in the AuCu3 configuration. Moreover, the electronic density of states and magnetic properties around the Fermi level are largely consistent across configurations. The proposed GdxCm1-xSn3 alloy exhibits magnetic properties similar to the parent compounds, and our findings suggest it has potential applications in the development of exotic superconductors and magnetic materials. Reconstructing cosmological parameters relying on the cosmological evolution of Type Ia Supernovae (SNe Ia) rely on mapping their luminosity distortion due to gravitational lensing caused by foreground mass structures. We calculated this effect for the largest SNe Ia datasets available, utilizing a simple model that accounts for the statistical properties of lensing distortions. Our findings indicate that the average magnification of the Pantheon SN Ia sample is extremely small, approximately 0.001 mag. When combined with its intrinsic scatter, it is negligible in comparison. As a result, the limited additional information provided by lensing distortions means that their impact on the estimation of cosmological parameters from SNe Ia data is minimal. Consequently, any potential bias introduced by underlying assumptions in our lensing model will be insignificant in comparison to other errors in such analyses. Our research was based on a new analytical lensing model that incorporates the effects of SNe Ia host galaxies being located within the centers of lenses. We found that the rare occurrence of this effect means it has a negligible influence on the distribution of lensing distortions induced by foreground structures. Therefore, both this situation and the general weakness of lensing distortions mean that our analysis, and hence these effects, are relevant for current SN Ia datasets but will become less significant in future datasets affected by lenses in the line of sight that include hosted galaxies. Our lensing distortion model is straightforward and lacks the complex variability seen in some simulations of the effect. While stronger lensing distortions may reveal more intricate patterns, even the basic model successfully reproduces the relationship between SN Ia luminosity distortions and the mass of the foreground lenses. Additionally, both this model and more sophisticated variations will be applicable to future SN Ia datasets affected by the effects of gravitational lensing in the line of sight. Our research used the Pantheon SN Ia dataset combined with a dataset that simulates the effect of lensing on such data. The silicon-on-insulator material possession has been developed to address the challenges associated with silicon integration, and it has demonstrated considerable potential in creating compact, low-loss, and high-speed optical devices. This report outlines the theoretical foundations for implementing T-shaped add-drop modules within the SOI structure, and it predicts a suitable operation regime for these modules. A 500nm x 500nm T hub with a 1.5μm etched depth exhibits an over 10dB optical signal processing capacity across a 300nm width range. Furthermore, this device displays minimal crosstalk, with a 10dB threshold within a 400nm length range due to its rectangular structure. This T hub's reduced size and low crosstalk make it suitable for high-density silicon integrated platforms, and it can be combined with other silicon integrated devices through fusion bonding, providing that the material properties of the silicon materials complement each other. This combination could lead to the development of complex silicon integrated photonic circuits with massive capacity. The report also examines the T hub's wavelength add-drop functionality, revealing that it can efficiently process different wavelength signals by positioning the etched region at a 300nm distance from the T hub's ends, and that it exhibits a 1.5dB optical signal processing capacity across a 300nm width range. This allows for the creation of compact silicon integrated photonic devices with high capacity, specifically Wavelength Division Multiplexing add-drop modules. The report also examines the T hub's polarization add-drop functionality, revealing that it can efficiently process different polarization signals by positioning the etched region at a 1.5μm distance from the T hub's ends, and that it exhibits a 1.5dB optical signal processing capacity across a 300nm width range. This allows for the creation of compact silicon integrated photonic devices with high capacity, specifically Polarization Division Multiplexing add-drop modules. The report also examines the T hub's frequency add-drop functionality, revealing that it can efficiently process different frequency signals by positioning the etched region at a 300nm distance from the T hub's ends, and that it exhibits a 1.5dB optical signal processing capacity across a 300nm width range. This allows for the creation of compact silicon integrated photonic devices with high capacity, specifically Frequency Division Multiplexing add-drop modules. The report also examines the T hub's phase add-drop functionality, revealing that it can efficiently process different phase signals by positioning the etched region at a 300nm distance from the T hub

In our analysis of a context-aware object recognition system using a pre-trained neural network, we found that the majority of misclassified objects were misclassified due to errors in the neural network itself, rather than misclassification caused by the context. We used a more precise metric that accounted for the network's own mistakes and found that the context's accuracy was approximately 1-2% higher than this adjusted metric. We believe this small gain might not be sufficient to support the claim that context is particularly beneficial for a neural network with current high performance levels. We also discovered instances where the context incorrectly labeled objects that the neural network had identified correctly. We think these findings have implications for the ongoing research on context-aware object recognition and other computational tasks. We recommend further investigation into a more nuanced understanding of context's effectiveness by using methods that enable more precise assessments of context's influence. We have made our code and data available for others to build upon in the Open Source Code section. We have also explored two alternative context-aware object recognition system designs, neither of which involved training the neural network on context. Our findings are relevant to both on-board and remote recognition systems. We think there are other areas such as action recognition, speech recognition, and natural language processing that our analysis may have implications for. We believe our analysis has value beyond just the specific context-aware object recognition system we tested, and has been neutral towards the particular network architecture that was used, which was a ResNet-50. We think our analysis has value for other network architectures such as Inception, VGGNet, and MobileNet. We think our analysis has value for other network architectures that were not mentioned in the paper. We think our analysis has value for other tasks such as the specific object recognition task we tested, but also for other object recognition tasks such as the recognition of animals, the recognition of people, the recognition of vehicles, the recognition of ships, the recognition of aircraft, the recognition of generic objects, the recognition of characters, and the recognition of symbols. We examine the convergence of the empirical measures resulting from independent
samples drawn from two distributions over binary random variables with negative
correlation. Our research reveals that the shape of the correlation function
determines the rate at which the total variation distance between the empirical
measures converges to the difference between the two underlying measures. In
particular, when the correlation function has a certain structure, we can
establish an upper bound on the total variation distance that follows an
exponential rate of convergence. Additionally, our findings related to
exponential decay are applicable to a specific class of distributions that
incorporate the Euler-Maclaurin series and its generalizations, as well as the
Gaillard-Shi inequality, thereby providing an alternative proof of these
results. We also investigate the convergence of the empirical measures in the
Hellinger distance, obtaining an upper bound that scales with the square root
of the number of samples, and demonstrating that this bound can be sharp in
the context of certain complex-valued distributions over finite spaces. Our
research further includes a concentration inequality that extends the
Varadhan-Sanov LDP to arbitrarily structured functions, ensuring its applicability
to binary random variables, and providing an alternative proof of the
Gaillard-Shi inequality, as well as an independent derivation of the Euler-
Maclaurin series LDP. Lastly, we establish an upper bound on the expected
square of the total variation distance between the empirical measures and the
difference between the two underlying measures, which can be minimized by
adjusting the sampling distribution, and we provide an illustrative example for
this phenomenon. Our main statistical application involves estimating the
difference between two underlying measures based on dependent samples, for which
we introduce an adjustment that can lead to improved estimates, and we also
investigate the concentration of the empirical measures around the estimated
parameter, obtaining an exponential decay rate of convergence. Moreover, our
research includes a concentration inequality that extends the Varadhan-Sanov LDP
to arbitrarily structured functions, ensuring its applicability to binary random
variables, and providing an alternative proof of the Gaillard-Shi inequality,
as well as an independent derivation of the Euler-Maclaurin series LDP, which
can be applied to concentrate expectations of functions of the empirical
measure. Lastly, we provide an intuitive yet mathematical formulation of the

Given a closed and oriented surface of genus greater than zero, a symplectic alteration is a method for transforming any valid symplectic field on this surface into another valid symplectic field through a series of local transformations. These local transformations can turn a point of contact in a field that is not proper onto a point of contact in a proper field, or change the orientation of a field that is proper. Our research shows that there are no algorithms available to automatically perform these alterations for all surfaces, demonstrating that implementing such an algorithm would result in a contradiction. Additionally, we provide evidence suggesting that even for the simplest surfaces, performing these alterations is not a computationally efficient process. A more complex variant of these alterations, known as pseudo-holomorphic alterations, also shares these properties and consequences.

The recent introduction of incompatible kidney transplants from living donors has posed significant challenges to implantation strategies. While multiple kidney transplants from the same donor can be syngenic, other transplants may require immunosuppression and pose a greater disease transmission risk. To optimize transplant outcomes for both recipients and the living donor, we propose a new method of selecting the best kidney pairings for acceptance. This method considers not only blood type compatibility but also other factors such as tissue typing, organ function, and disease transmission risk. We have further incorporated tools like allocation systems to prioritize certain transplants over others. Our method aims to minimize rejection risk, disease transmission risk, and immunosuppression required while maximizing the number of acceptable kidney transplants. This has been mathematically proven to provide the ideal acceptance of kidney pairs in a general setting. However, with increased complexity, it can potentially become computationally challenging. To address this, we have further developed a more streamlined and efficient version of the method. This newer version has been successfully applied to real-world scenarios involving living donor kidney transplants. It has also been compared to existing methods to demonstrate its benefits. This research can be extended to other organ transplants with living donors. The proposed method can be tailored to suit various situations and environments. This has significant implications for various allocation systems used globally. It has further highlighted the importance of accessing blood type and tissue typing information for living donor kidney pairs. This can be achieved by either providing discounted or free testing to living donors. This research has been conducted in close collaboration with transplant professionals. It has also raised various ethical and practical considerations that require further investigation. This can be achieved through multi-disciplinary research involving fields like computer science, medicine, economics, and ethics. This has further highlighted the complexity of kidney transplant allocation decisions. This has been demonstrated by both mathematical and computational evidence. It has further shown that such decisions can vary significantly from optimal solutions. This has implications for other allocation decision-making problems involving constraints and priorities. This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word representations learned through the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Dictionary, a widely used resource for capturing the emotional content of words. We question the uniform distribution assumption of word representations across this dictionary's polarity spectrum and test it using a variety of statistical methods. Our findings suggest that the representations do not adhere to a uniform pattern and instead exhibit a more complex, often nonlinear relationship with the dictionary's polarities. This article presents SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM schemes that mimic the beneficial consequences of our previously proposed WBWFC structure, leveraging wideband frequency domains to gain additional advantages beyond multiple antennas and carriers. By dividing a wide bandwidth into narrowband signals, these models also offer reduced dynamic power and increased signal-to-noise ratio. We show that SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM are analogous to our WBWFC structure, enabling us to utilize existing WBWFC performance results to convey performance benefits of these new schemes. Moreover, we derive explicit performance results for SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM, covering both ideal and real-world conditions. These results demonstrate the superior performance of these schemes in compared simulations. The findings related to SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM can be applied to various scenarios, including combined systems, multiple access scenarios, and coexistence problems. The positive outcomes of these schemes encourage further innovation in integrated data and power transfer systems. The performance results and condition-based derivations of SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM also contribute to the scientific community. The code for the proposed schemes and corresponding simulation environments are available online. This study introduces a hybrid level-set / embedded boundary method to address problems associated with moving boundaries in solidification-melt scenarios. By incorporating the level-set and embedded boundary approaches, we've developed a technique that leverages the strengths of both methods, combining the level-set method's ability to handle smooth interfaces with the embedded boundary approach's simplicity in handling complex geometry. This hybrid technique eliminates the need for the strict orientation convention inherent in the level-set method and allows for the use of standard finite element methods on the interface. This method also maintains conservation of mass and temperature conservation during solidification-melt problems. To validate this hybrid approach, we compared it with the level-set method and observed similar results. Furthermore, we tested this method against published studies involving phase change problems and found it to be accurate. This hybrid technique has been applied to a range of problems, including Stefan problems, dendrite growth, and melting problems with convective heat transfer. To round out this study, we discussed possible extensions and modifications to this method, including implementing contact line dynamics and resolving the 3D Taylor problem. This hybrid technique has the potential to be a more efficient and simpler level-set method, and we have made the code available publicly. In multiagent competitions, players' motivations can be driven by a mix of cooperative and self-serving intentions.  When encountering others who may be cooperative or manipulate them, individuals should strike a balance between collaborative behavior and deceptive actions.  We examine a rationalizable strategy for players to reach a cooperative equilibrium in a game involving multiple competitors, focusing on a model where others' past behaviors can be perceived as rational or intended to deceive.  We establish that players using a straightforward approach can identify cooperative equilibria in various games through observation of others' past actions.  However, we also identify instances in which cooperative equilibria are impossible to determine as others' intentions may be uncertain.  Furthermore, we analyze the relationship between cooperative equilibria and stable states in response to a change in payoffs, finding that it adheres to a specific rule.  In a dynamic setting, we demonstrate that cooperative equilibria can be acquired at a finite point in time, and that the time it takes is directly linked to the degree of uncertainty existing due to others' possible intentions.  Lastly, we discuss a key distinction between two variants of a game, one that incorporates a form of positive assurance, as well as the implications of this difference for cooperative equilibria and stable states.  This is in addition to examining how a change in payoffs affects these states.  We conclude by examining the connection between cooperative equilibria and stable states in a special type of game, one that represents an evolutionary scenario.  In this context, we find that cooperative equilibria and stable states coincide, unlike in traditional evolutionary games.  On the other hand, we also find that a change in payoffs can result in a transition to a state that is unstable, although this is preceded by a period of uncertainty.  This uncertainty is caused by the possibility of deceptive actions being performed by some individuals. Integrating diverse datasets, stemming from data and theoretical sources, is a prerequisite for accurately fitting probability density functions. While aligning the format of experimental data is a straightforward process, reconciling disparate theoretical predictions is a more complex task. This document is intended to provide guidelines for conforming theoretical predictions to a standardized format, compatible with the PDF fitting framework. Specifically, it outlines the necessary steps to convert a wide variety of predictions, including those from effective field theories, unitary gauge treatments, and multicomponent density matrix formulations, into a uniform format suitable for incorporation into the PDF fitting framework. By standardizing theoretical predictions in this manner, researchers can easily combine their results with experimental data in the context of PDF fitting, thus facilitating a more comprehensive understanding of physical phenomena. This theory framework is particularly well-suited for applications involving PDF fitting and is relevant to a broad range of research areas, including but not limited to QCD, effective field theories, and neutrino physics. It is further emphasized that this document focuses exclusively on theoretical predictions and does not address the integration of experimental data. By conforming to this protocol, researchers can easily share their theoretical predictions, either publicly or privately, through a web-based portal hosted by the PDF fitting group. This initiative is part of a broader project aimed at developing a flexible and automated framework for PDF fitting, tailored to meet the needs of both researchers and members of the neutrino community. This document is structured to facilitate clear understanding, with detailed information presented in the form of appendices. It is worthwhile to note that this theory framework has been applied successfully in the context of neutrino PDF fitting, as demonstrated by the results presented in the accompanying paper "Neutral kaon physics at $O(a^2$) in lattice QCD". This research investigates an intricate problem involving acoustic forcing of a turbulent jet flame in an enclosed space. When a jet flame burns within a confined environment, it can sometimes experience instability issues due to the interplay between its outer boundary, flame structure, and buoyancy force. To better understand this complex phenomenon, a two-dimensional linearized model is proposed to study this interaction. The proposed model divides the flow field into two separate regions - an inner region near the flame where equations are solved using nonlinear reaction diffusion equations, and an outer region where acoustic fluctuations dominate and are described by linear oscillatory equations. The two regions are connected through a matching procedure based on the asymptotic properties of the nonlinear solution near the flame. In order to obtain the linearized equations for the outer region, the model is further developed to include an active flame method, where the flame reacts to acoustic waves by changing its structure, and vice versa. This proposed model then is applied to a variety of scenarios, such as those with acoustic forcing, near a solid wall, or in situations where the flame attaches itself to the wall. In all cases, the results obtained from the linearized model are compared with existing nonlinear simulations. In one specific scenario, the reduction from a two-dimensional nonlinear model to a linearized model leads to a significant computational savings of about 100 times. In addition to its applications, this research also highlights the capabilities of the active flame method and the linearized model in capturing key features of a jet flame burning in an enclosed space. In particular, the research shows that the active flame method is capable of reproducing the observed phenomenon of a jet flame becoming unstable at a certain distance from the surface it is burning near. In one specific instance, this distance threshold is equal to half the length of the enclosure. Using a comprehensive database of genomic regions, functional attributes and annotations, a comprehensive framework has been developed to investigate the integrated data and identify significant associations between genomic regions and the traits.  This analysis has been applied to public data sets regarding gene expression, histone modification, DNA methylation, and chromatin structure across 14 human tissues.  The analysis of gene expression weights the importance of genes based on their expression levels across different tissues, thereby enhancing the detection of a majority of validated associations and confirming that the majority of genome-wide associations are true.  On the other hand, the analysis of histone modification, DNA methylation, and chromatin structure weights the importance of genomic regions based on their accessibility or modification status across different cells and tissues, thereby providing insights into the biological mechanisms governing the traits. However, extracting information about the underlying dynamics is challenging due to the overwhelming influence of these substructure components, especially in the forward direction. We define a domain to have a well-respected domain structure if its valuation ring contains a subring with a well-defined residue map and integrally dominates the original domain. We then establish that in the context of a domain with a well-respected domain structure, its total quotient ring equals the quotient of its valuation ring by this residue map. Furthermore, this property is shown to be equivalent to the domain's localizations at its prime ideals possessing a well-defined residue map. Additionally, we prove that domains with a well-respected domain structure are precisely those that only have prime ideals with a well-defined residue map. In the process, we also demonstrate that this property is hereditary, meaning it is inherited by the domain's localizations at its prime ideals. In order to make efficient use of power-consuming CPU frequencies, a new approach is proposed in this research. A GPU-accelerated methodology is developed to determine the optimal CPU frequency schedule, considering various workload characteristics and different power consumption models. The proposed strategy, called HyperDegrade, utilizes machine learning to identify relevant workload features and a binary integer programming model to find the ideal frequency schedule. The results of HyperDegrade demonstrate significant performance improvements in frequency consolidation: on one hand, when using real workload data, the efficiency of CPU frequency schedule reaches 98% on average; on the other hand, in fictitious scenarios simulating real applications, the methodology achieves an average speedup of 12 times and an average energy reduction of 90% in the GPU environment, and an average speedup of 7 times and an average energy reduction of 80% in the bare-metal environment. The researchers also tested HyperDegrade on real systems by deploying the GPU-based methodology on an open-source benchmark platform, and found that in addition to reducing energy consumption, the methodology is capable of discovering hidden bottlenecks in workloads, as well as providing accurate prediction capabilities. The research shows that there is plenty of room for optimizing CPU frequency schedules, and that HyperDegrade opens up new avenues for research in this area. The researchers provide the methodology and benchmark data of HyperDegrade on the website of the IEEE/ACM CCGrid conference. Our approach involves developing a systematic method to assess the effectiveness of these rule-based collaborations and identifying specific scenarios where such approaches are optimal. Experimental evaluations, conducted using simulated and actual networks, validate our findings and demonstrate the feasibility of our approach in complex settings. In this work, we introduce a novel concept called Pragmatic Privacy Assaults (PPAs), which involves a malicious agent feeding certain private information to a machine learning model in a centralized setting, with the purpose of impairing its effectiveness when deployed on a related task in a different context. We then discuss how PPAs can be employed to hinder model performance in situations where data is limited, such as in the course of vertical federated learning. We outline specific strategies a malicious participant might use to compromise a model in a federated learning framework, including manipulating a model trained on their data to make it less accurate when applied to a different dataset. We also examine various scenarios in which PPAs could occur, including situations where data is restricted and people are willing to share limited information about themselves. Moreover, we investigate the connection between PPAs and other attacks, such as manipulation of features and attribute hacking, and provide guidance on how to anticipate and counter PPA attacks. Finally, we outline potential solutions, including implementing more rigorous security protocols, as well as ways to prevent PPA attacks and detect them in progress. Overall, PPA attacks highlight the complexities and challenges of developing secure, practical machine learning models in a centralized or federated setting. The issue of PPA attacks also raises important questions about data privacy, especially in a world where people are increasingly willing to share limited information about themselves. The research reported here has been conducted in a centralized setting, but its findings also apply to the specific case of vertical federated learning, and the concepts it introduces will be relevant to other contexts, such as protocol attacks and manipulation of machine learning models through pre-training. The study of PPA attacks offers insights that can be used to improve the security of machine learning models, including recommending additional validation tests to carry out during the development stage, as well as evaluating the risk of PPA attacks and identifying areas in which they are likely to occur. The work reported here is relevant to a broad range of fields, including artificial intelligence, machine learning, statistics, computer science, and operations research, and can be applied to a wide range of domains, including genetics, finance, and sociology. We introduce the concept of Random Fourier Traits (RFTs), a connection between Random Fourier Features (RFFs) and the Traits of the characteristic function of a Gaussian distribution. We utilize this connection to create data-dependent kernel estimation based on the characteristics of RFTs. This approach leads to reduced storage needs compared to traditional RFF methods while maintaining computational efficiency in tasks like matrix multiplication. Furthermore, we enhance our data-dependent method to accommodate multi-class kernel ridge regression challenges. Throughout this research, we leveraged the RFTs framework to create an efficient and adaptable kernel estimation framework, demonstrating the benefits of analyzing kernel methods through the lens of statistical traits. This work was previously published in the proceedings of the 10th International Conference on Machine Learning and Applications. We also developed a Python implementation of the proposed method, available for public use. We derive an explicit formula for the scalar curvature $R_m$ in terms of $u$, establish a lower bound for $R_m$ in terms of a norm related to the gradient of $u$, and a upper bound for a related norm related to the $L^p$ norm of $u$ and its derivatives. Additionally, we classify hypersurfaces with constant M\"obius scalar curvature under specific transformation conditions. Furthermore, we provide an alternative approach to classifying hypersurfaces with constant mean curvature under these conditions. We also analyze the stability of the stiffness of M\"obius scalar curvature hypersurfaces and derive an inequality involving a norm related to the second derivative of $u$ and the $L^p$ norm of $u$ and its derivatives. We conclude by investigating the relationship between the M\"obius scalar curvature and the regularity of hypersurfaces in the context of an inverse problem. A Cayley tree model is a random graph model consisting of nodes with degrees defined by a probability distribution, where two nodes are connected if their degrees satisfy a specified condition. We examine the probability distribution of the number of node deletions required to reduce the degree of a random node to zero in a large, densely packed Cayley tree. Using the percolation theory, we derive an expression for the average number of node deletions needed, along with the standard deviation of this quantity. As the degree of the tree increases, we find that the standard deviation becomes negligible compared to the average, and the distribution of the number of node deletions approaches a Poisson distribution. This phenomenon has been observed in simulations for a variety of degree distributions. The conditions under which the distribution of the number of node deletions changes to a Poisson distribution are yet to be determined. Along with this, we also investigate the average number of node deletions needed to remove all nodes of a particular degree in the Cayley tree. This generalizes the earlier results of Brunet and Derrida, whose percolation-based approach we replicate through an alternate argument from the flow equation. This newer analysis of the problem is accompanied by an additional example of a degree distribution, whose associated percolation theory provides an analytic expression for the average number of node deletions needed. This particular degree distribution can be realized through a iterative process known as the Eden model. This model starts with a single node and repeatedly adds new nodes connected to existing ones at random, until the model reaches a state where no new nodes can be added. This process results in a Cayley tree with a power-law degree distribution, whose exponent measures the standard deviation of the number of node deletions required to reduce the degree of a random node to zero in the limit of a large, densely packed tree. This phenomenon has further been confirmed through simulations of the Eden model. This simulation confirms that the distribution of the number of node deletions needed to reduce the degree of a random node to zero in the limit of a large, densely packed tree is a Poisson distribution, for a variety of different exponents in the power-law degree distribution. This simulation also compares the average number of node deletions needed to remove all nodes of a particular degree in the Cayley tree with the results obtained from the percolation theory, and finds them to be in close agreement with each other. The detection of gravitational waves at high frequencies is limited by the presence of laser noise in optical interferometric detectors. To enhance the performance in the frequency range beyond 100 Hz, we examine the potential of modifying the antenna design to include a sloshing fluid in a Sagnac interferometer configuration. By analyzing the dynamics of the fluid in the cavity, we identify a controllable reservoir that can be utilized to remove noise components affecting the detector. The effectiveness of this noise-reducing approach has been successfully demonstrated in simulations, resulting in a significant improvement in end instrument sensitivity by a factor of twenty in the frequency range between 100 and 500 Hz. This innovation offers a versatile means of enhancing the sensitivity of optical interferometric detectors employed in the detection of gravitational waves. Furthermore, this finding holds value for the broad scope of opto-mechanical systems employing cavities with a slow lyapunov time, across various applications. The implementation of this technology in operating detectors such as LIGO, Virgo, and future detectors like Einstein Telescope and third-generation LIGO, among others, is relatively straightforward and can yield a 10-fold improvement in sensitivity above the 100 Hz mark. The implications of this discovery for the design of future detectors are substantial, with potential designs like the described sloshing-Sagnac antenna offering an appealing alternative to similar designs based on recycling Michelson interferometers. The associated code is publicly accessible via GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/Aydar-Sabirov/Sloshing-Sagnac. The code is written in C++ and utilizes the NumPy and SciPy libraries, with the results verified against the original MATLAB code provided by Dr. R. Cotestato. The proposed design has been physically validated at the University of Michigan, with the code also utilized in the simulation of a recently proposed novel design called the Leaning-Sloshing-Sagnac antenna. The associated data is publicly available via Harvard Dataverse at the following link: https://dataverse.harvard.edu/dataset.xhtml?persistentId=doi:10.7910/dw.com/psycm_ua8mw. Researchers explored the potential of large-scale multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) technology in thickly populated urban environments and discovered that its performance could be significantly enhanced by adjusting the base station's antenna configuration to match the local geometric features. However, determining the optimal configuration remains challenging due to the complex non-linear relationship between MIMO performance and urban geometry. In the course of investigating this issue, an interesting phenomenon was observed - a specific arrangement of antennas, positioned at different heights, creates overlapping visibility zones that, in turn, result in reduced performance. To further examine this peculiar effect, we studied the intersection of these overlapping areas, representing the region where two separate Cellular Networks can share the same coverage without experiencing signal interference. In the process, we developed mathematical formulas to define the static boundaries of these overlapping areas and tracked the dynamics of these boundaries in random scenarios. Combining these insights with stochastic modeling, we developed a practical algorithm to optimize the antenna configuration and thus enhance the MIMO performance in urban settings. In the process, we discovered a specific arrangement - the 'V' shape - which has been shown to provide superior performance in various scenarios. The research was conducted in the frequency band of 5.9 GHz, commonly used in urban areas, and the results were verified through actual measurements in a controlled environment. The findings have important implications for the design of future MIMO technology, particularly in crowded urban environments, and provide a practical solution for base station antenna configuration that could be adapted for other frequency bands. The discovery of the unique phenomenon of non-intersecting visibility areas in MIMO technology also opens up new areas of research, such as the performance of these systems in three-dimensional environments and the effects of different antenna configurations on the overlapping areas. The results of the research have been physically verified and the findings published in the journal IEEE Antennas and Wireless Propagation Letters under the title 'Non-Intersecting Visibility Areas in XL-MIMO Stochastic Access Protocol' along with the associated algorithm published in the journal IEEE Communications Letters under the title 'V-Shaped Antenna Configuration in Urban XL-MIMO Environment'. The research was conducted by a team of graduate students led by the supervisor Mohammed Al-Dhelba. The results of the research have been recognized internationally and have led to significant interest from the mobile industry. The discovery of the unique phenomenon of non-intersecting visibility areas in MIMO technology was recognized as one of the top scientific achievements of 2023 by the international organization known as IOP Publishing. Initially, a demonstration of a frequency-stable M{\o}lmer-S{\o}rensen gate is performed using two equally weighted qubit states and two symmetrically populated motional modes. The resulting gate operation maintains its accuracy despite the motional mode frequency drifts. The requirement for equal mode weighting is eliminated by designing a specific motional state preparation procedure, allowing for the creation of frequency-stable controlled-Z gates with uniform amplitude and phase, even in the presence of motional mode frequency drifts. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through the accurate execution of a Shor algorithm circuit. Our analysis is centered on theoretical investigations to design a highly connected Dirac material, utilizing graphene's surface functionality as the foundation, with surface nitrogen vacancies serving as scattering sources to break the symmetry and create an all-inclusive band structure characteristic of this class of materials. By modeling the interaction between an electron and a phonoion, a composite entity formed by an electron and a phonon, our research reveals the fundamental principles required to overcome the limitations of massless Dirac electrons, even when they are scattered by defects or imperfections. Consequently, we examine the implications for a hexagonal boron nitride layer, already known for its exceptional stability, lacking free carriers, and robust symmetry in its vibrational spectrum. To achieve the desired effect, we propose introducing a carbon doped phonio, resulting from the replacement of some nitrogen atoms with carbon, which forms a bond with neighboring nitrogen atoms, altering the local geometry sufficiently to break the symmetry and create a gap in the band structure. Alternatively, we investigate the effect of edge locations of surface functional groups on the connectivity of a hexagonal lattice, edge sharing with the carbon atoms, and propose several candidates, including oxygen, sulfur, and selenium. In both scenarios, our calculations indicate that a gap can be created through appropriate placement of scatterers or functional groups on the surface, maintaining an association with the Dirac band structure even when scattered by defects or imperfections. Furthermore, our research predicts that such a material would exhibit unusual properties, both in its static and dynamic responses, potentially allowing for the detection of a Dirac cone in an experiment, as well as facilitating the development of theories for interacting electrons in a phonio system. Lastly, we outline a protocol for experimental verification, including a characterization of the static and dynamic responses via scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy, and propose that all-inclusive band structures be considered a universal feature of Dirac materials, capable of being robustly maintained even in the presence of defects or imperfections.

The proposal for the 750 GeV upgrade of the CERN neutrino beam line known as the Beam Dump Experiment (BDE) aims to greatly reduce neutrino flux at the experiment's detection point while increasing the sensitivity to dark sectors. A key aspect of this setup is the nearly collision-free high-intensity beam of charged hadrons hitting the target. To take advantage of this setup, researchers are re-examining decay processes of various particles, even if they were previously overlooked due to the presence of background neutrinos. This paper focuses on determining the expected detection efficiency for the decay of neutral mesons, specifically neutral kaons, into a electron and a neutral particle, assuming this decay involves the generation of neutral leptons. By comparing the expected rate of this decay to be approximately 10^7 per second, it's clear that a cut-off needs to be implemented to prevent neutral kaons that decay into neutral leptons and then back into kaons from being misclassified. This cut-off would likely occur at a mass threshold of 50 MeV for neutral leptons. As a result, researchers are re-evaluating the proposed BDE detector for its ability to detect neutral kaons with a specific range of masses, a task that can be achieved by increasing the magnetic field of the return yoke from 3.85 to 5.75 T. This change is expected to improve the detection efficiency for these masses by a factor of 10, primarily due to a significant reduction in misidentified neutral kaons. This, in turn, will allow the experiment to place more restrictive limits on the product of the neutral kaon coupling constant and its branching ratio into a neutral lepton, a achievement for masses less than 83 MeV, with a breakthrough for the first time in the mass range between 10-83 MeV. Furthermore, this detection capability is expected to extend to other rare decays of neutral hadrons, such as the decay of neutral mesons into a muon and a neutral particle. This development also highlights the importance of accurately calculating the production and decay spectra of these particles, as well as the effects of polarization on neutral kaon decays, particularly for decays involving neutral leptons. This discovery has the potential to enable a wide range of physics research, including the investigation of composite dark sectors, as well as the study of neutral lepton masses, and will continue to inspire new ideas for improving the detector's performance, such as utilizing a more sophisticated magnetic field design to further enhance the detection efficiency. Neural language models have largely surpassed $N$-gram models due to better performance, but our findings suggest that $n$-gram models still excel in many situations with low computational costs, demonstrating a strong foundation of language understanding. Building upon this discovery, we developed a neural model that learns from the remaining knowledge between $n$-gram models and the true language distribution, allowing for both a deeper grasp of language and the flexibility to adjust models through the $n$-gram base without altering the neural model. Through extensive experiments on tasks including language modeling, machine translation, and summarization, our hybrid approach consistently delivers enhanced performance over standard neural models and facilitates seamless domain adaptation by simply swapping the $n$-gram base, eliminating the need for additional training. Our code has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghrua/NgramRes.

Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial details, particularly in images depicting large head orientations. This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To break down this complex task into more manageable components, our approach focuses on predicting two overlapping faces from a single image, with each predicted face possessing a distinct orientation. We demonstrate that modeling facial geometry as a pair of overlapping spheres improves the representation of head poses and provides a suitable framework for representing and differentiating extreme head orientations. Furthermore, we introduce a self-alignment mechanism among the predicted faces, which facilitates incremental head-pose learning and enhances the robustness of our method. We also introduce a non-occluded reference point on the face for unambiguous labeling of head orientations and implement a simple yet effective strategy for handling dense correspondences in low-texture face regions. We validate our approach through extensive experimentation on the AFLW2000-3D and Florence datasets, yielding superior performance in terms of reconstruction accuracy and robustness in challenging head-pose scenarios. We also apply our method to the task of 3D face alignment and obtain state-of-the-art results on the widely-used ABFW dataset. We make our code publicly available at: https://github.com/zhengyangzhang/SADRNet.

This investigation seeks to examine the capabilities of Informed Optical Character Recognition (iOCR) in accurately counting election ballots, focusing on a dataset provided by the Kansas Secretary of State's Office. To evaluate iOCR's performance, two approaches were utilized: a traditional method performing character-level recognition and a statistical method based on handwriting analysis, respectively. The study found that iOCR achieved a 99.97% accuracy rate in counting ballots, and a 94.44% accuracy rate in calculating election results. Moreover, a comparison with a conventional OCR system revealed that iOCR outperformed the conventional system in this context. The research was conducted in collaboration with the Kansas Secretary of State's Office, and the findings have been applied to count the results of a real election. In this research, we examine the ability of linear models with interlingual parameters and temporal data to successfully forecast future observations. We demonstrate that certain models, even with an excess of parameters, can accurately predict future data by leveraging experiences from past observations. We show that the performance of these models isn't hindered when using a large amount of data, and that they can anticipate observations beyond the data used for training with a growing number of parameters. We discover that the reduction in prediction error over time isn't linear and that linear regression isn't an accurate representation of this relationship. We develop a new theoretical framework that explains how models with interlingual parameters and temporal data interact, and it differs from the standard temporal regression framework. We discover that the reduction in prediction error is controlled by the ratio of the number of parameters to the sample size, and that it's influenced by the diversity of the data and the model. We propose a new temporal linear model with interlingual parameters and regularization techniques to make it more reliable and accurate, and we provide theoretical guarantees for its performance. We also conduct a comprehensive set of experiments to evaluate the performance of this model on real and synthetic data, and the results show that it consistently outperforms standard temporal linear models. A key challenge in the integration of renewable energy sources lies in managing seasonal fluctuations, which can be addressed through advanced storage systems. As storage technology improves, there's a growing interest in self-planning energy storage on an individual basis, without relying on utility companies. However, determining the optimal storage capacity requires considering various factors including financial returns, consumption patterns, and the dynamics of local energy markets, which can be unpredictable. Existing storage planning methods often overlook real-time market fluctuations, focusing instead on historical consumption and price data. In this study, a cautious self-planning approach for storage is presented, taking into account both cautious consumption and production strategies and a market risk preference that reflects the risk associated with selling or storing energy. A risk-neutral valuation technique is used to value storage, combining utility companies' tariffs and the potential risks and benefits of selling or storing energy. A simulated example using a prosumer with a solar panel array demonstrates how this approach can be applied, and shows that a perfect forward market reduces the risk and increases the value of storage, while a retail market tariff scheme such as the German "Energiewende" leads to over-storage. This paper delves into the underlying causes for the limited success of distant similar learning methods. It appears that current approaches are unable to effectively tackle classification problems at the scale of ImageNet, due to performance being hindered by a significant drop of at least 4%. It is hypothesized that this decline is resultant from the loss of difficult data examples occurring under distant similar learning. To address this issue, the paper introduces a new task called dynamic learning, which places harder examples at the disposal of more capable models. It is demonstrated that this novel framework is effective in absorbing challenging data, thereby expanding the subset of difficult examples available to the standard model by at least 13%. Furthermore, this approach is shown to yield comparable performance to the capable model, with results being validated across multiple classification tasks including ResNet, ReLU based models and on large-scale datasets such as ImageNet. The findings are then utilized to demonstrate the relationship between distant similar learning and the difficulty of data, which is a key aspect in the theory of the framework. Finally, the paper also presents a list of open questions in this area of research. In Dynamic Time-Division Duplexing (TDD), base stations can adjust their transmission schedules independently to accommodate varying traffic demands, but this leads to interference between the uplink and downlink channels and incurs significant performance costs. To mitigate this effect, this work develops a non-Coordination and non-Verifiable (NCV) game-theoretic scheduling framework to dynamically manage TDD configurations at base stations within a 5G network. The NCV framework ensures that players' rational self-interest-driven scheduling decisions result in a Nash Equilibrium, which approximates an optimal solution obtainable from a formulated mixed-integer linear programming problem. The introduction of a temporary reference signal allows for efficient resolution of player identities, reducing the spectral costs of cell configuration updates. Furthermore, this research includes an appealing discussion on the convergence of the proposed greedy algorithm and the computational efficiency of various cell-configuring strategies. The developed framework is thoroughly evaluated through extensive simulations, revealing its superiority over static TDD scheduling strategies. The results show that the proposed NCV game-theoretic scheduling framework delivers a 20% performance improvement over a basic random scheduling approach and reduces the system's spectral costs by a 30% margin in dense networks. We demonstrate how to obtain linear and affine approximations of such networks by establishing their connection to multilayer perceptrons. Furthermore, we show that networks with a specific structure, having orthogonal weights and no bias terms, yield gradient information directly. Lastly, we outline the implications of our findings for optimizing Hamiltonian neural networks and highlight potential applications in utilizing gradient information for improved robustness and safety in critical systems. Our approach and results are illustrated through numerical examples including a simple nonlinear time-series prediction scenario and a more complex case involving a Hamiltonian neural network with a loop connection.
