Word Sense Discrimination (WSD) aims to determine the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings based on its context.  Despite significant progress in deep learning, distinguishing word senses remains challenging, especially in contexts lacking relevant information.  To address this difficulty, it is suggested that glossals, lists of words with their meanings, be integrated into models to facilitate WSD.  This study explores the potential benefits of combining context and glossals in models and investigates methods to enhance glossals for improved performance.  It is discovered that utilizing a simple and effective technique called Distributional Thesaurus Learning (DTL) to enrich glossals leads to superior outcomes in comparison to standard methods.  DTL generates glossals with expanded entries by incorporating related words derived from the distribution of words in a corpus.  It is demonstrated that models trained on context and modified glossals achieve the best results, outperforming standard models by a 7.5 percentage point margin in accurate sense identification.  This study on Word Sense Discrimination also contributes a newly created dataset consisting of 20 categories and 13,000 entries, alongside a software tool for managing the dataset and experimenting with various methods.  It is hoped that this research and the associated tools will stimulate future advancements in WSD.  Experimental results validation the findings involves verification through a combination of approaches, including the use of random forest, gold-standard selection, and the annotation of 500 instances by 8 different readers.  It is discovered that the most effective method of generating glossals for WSD involves selecting the most suitable sense of a word based on the information derived from the categories of a Thesaurus, followed by the inclusion of words that share the same characteristics as the original word, with the outcome of both approaches being validated through the creation of a new dataset consisting of 20 categories and 13,000 entries. Evaluating the Scientific Potential of Euclid's Legacy Survey for Cosmology, Euclid Inheritance, and other related surveys, this paper explores the consequences of reduced observing time on Euclid's capabilities and identifies ways to repurpose its existing design for enhanced scientific outcomes. By examining various scenarios, we evaluate the effects of altered observing times on cosmological measurements, incorporating factors such as survey periods, satellite positions, and ground-based observations. Our analysis focuses on the core goals of Euclid, namely probing dark matter and dark energy with accurate measurements of galaxy distributions and spectroscopic data. We investigate the potential of Euclid to meet these objectives in a range of scenarios, from reduced observing times to various survey designs, and explore ways to minimize the impact on its scientific outcomes. Furthermore, this study highlights the significance of long-term data storage and potential uses of Euclid data after the end of its operational period, including collaborations with other missions and surveys. By valuing the value of its legacy, Euclid can ensure a rich and productive post-mission life filled with new discoveries and scientific opportunities. We also outline specific ideas for Euclid's legacy studies, covering aspects such as atmospheric characterization, stellar parameters, and synergistic combinations with other missions and surveys. By examining these possibilities, we can ensure Euclid's data continues to contribute substantially to astronomical knowledge beyond the end of its planned operational period. This approach incorporates deterministic hydrodynamic equations coupled with noisy versions of the Balazs-Beloborodov-Ho noise sources, which arise in random phase space. We derived the specific stochastic equations characterizing long-wavelength fluctuations in time-dependent situations and during initial conditions. Furthermore, we introduced a quantum version of the Rayleigh instability indicator, which demonstrates that the stochastic theory is capable of reproducing the characteristics of quantum phases, including the onset of the Rayleigh instability and quantized circulation numbers. By applying the developed theory to describe noise in time-dependent situations and initial conditions, we obtained accurate fits to numerical results obtained using an exact solution for the one-dimensional semi-infinite Bose-Josephson model. This model exhibits both periodic and stationary regimes of behavior, with different fluctuation characteristics in various spatial locations. Our simulations demonstrate that our stochastic theory accurately captures the behavior of fluctuations in time-dependent situations and initial conditions, where spatial fluctuations appear to be smooth and hydrodynamic, whereas temporal fluctuations are more complex and stochastic. The occurrence of isospin breakdown in dense matter is thought to influence density dependence of neutron-proton imbalance, however, this relation remains poorly understood. A specific instance of isospin breakdown is described here, known as "form coexistence", which is characterized by coexisting quarks and hadrons at a single density in a high-isospin nucleus, namely 64Ni. Using relativistic mean-field models, researchers found that this scenario is explained by a specific interaction called the monopole tensor interaction, which overcomes obstacles that prevent it from successful use in relativistic mean-field theories. A distinctive characteristic of this interaction is that it causes a non-zero value of isospin-symmetric nuclear matter's incompressibility, which in turn allows for form coexistence to occur. A study found that the monopole tensor interaction primarily affects the neutron-proton ratio, although it also slightly affects the density dependence of this ratio. Furthermore, it was discovered that the density dependence of isospin-symmetric nuclear matter's pressure is affected by the monopole tensor interaction, though this effect is indirect and influenced by the Fock term. In summary, the unique properties of 64Ni make it an ideal candidate for exhibiting form coexistence, and it was found that this interaction is driven by the monopole tensor interaction, which influences the neutron-proton ratio and the pressure of isospin-symmetric nuclear matter. A related study used the monopole tensor interaction to investigate the isospin-breaking effects caused by the collapse of neutral kaon condensation in atomic nuclei, specifically in 28Si and 64Ni. Machine learning models, including those for NLP, are often adjusted for best performance by tweaking parameters such as learning rate and regularization. Despite the availability of efficient methods to achieve this optimal performance, a major challenge remains: the variance associated with these tuning processes. This variance complicates comparisons and placements of models in a hierarchical order. To address this issue, the community has been recommending the use of a hold-out method for validating the performance of the model. This paper argues that a jack-knife resampling method can be used to decrease the associated variance when comparing models, and that this method is particularly effective in comparing hierarchical distances between models. This is achieved by providing a formula that takes the variance associated with the tuning process and models the performance as normally distributed. This normal distribution is then utilized to conduct comparisons and placements of models in a hierarchical order based on certain criteria such as the ELBO score in VAEs. To support this paper's claims, an empirical study was conducted using a range of NLP tasks and models, including BERT and RoBERTa, which demonstrated a decrease in the associated variance when comparing models using the jack-knife resampling method. This reduction in variance enabled a more precise placement of models in a hierarchical order based on the ELBO score in VAEs. This paper's findings suggest that the community should consider using the jack-knife resampling method to decrease the associated variance when comparing models in a hierarchical order. This is particularly beneficial in situations where the difference between models is marginal, as it provides a more precise placement of models in a hierarchical order based on certain criteria such as the ELBO score in VAEs. This paper also highlights the importance of validating the normal distribution of the tuning process on real-world NLP tasks despite the limitations associated with this distribution. This survey explores educator-pupil frameworks with a focus on their underlying assumptions about knowledge and how it is structured, as well as the processes involved in knowledge acquisition. We examine different classifier-based educator-pupil structures, including multiple instances of Bayesian networks, decision trees, and other frameworks such as multi-agent systems, genetic algorithms, and neural networks. In evaluating these frameworks, we consider factors like accuracy, simplicity, and whether the knowledge is modulated during the learning process. This survey also delves into the related topics of knowledge acquisition, machine learning, and teaching systems, offering potential directions for developing a unified theory of knowledge and learning. Exact computation in graphical models is highly efficient when the models are structured as trees, but become cumbersome when they incorporate complex loops. One way to tackle this issue is by relying on variable elimination methods, yet even these can hit a roadblock with the presence of loops. Our novel approach, the Brief Function (BF) framework, takes a new perspective by directly managing the interplay between loops and marginalization. Given a model defined over a graph, the BF method generates a compact summary of the model's behavior at a particular query node. This summary takes the form of a simplified function that incorporates the effects of nearby factors and other marginalized nodes. We demonstrate how this new representation can be employed to achieve significant performance improvements in two key tasks. First, it accelerates the computation of the marginal posterior distribution under a given observation. Second, it enables the resolution of constraint-satisfaction problems in graphical models. Both of these applications benefit directly from the reduced complexity and loopy-free local structure captured by the Brief Function representation. In particular, we show how this representation can be used to develop a new algorithm for exact computation under loops, and also demonstrate its connection to existing variable elimination methods. In addition, we explore its connection to the dual blockwise tree representation of a graph, and provide a characterizations of graphs that can be adequately captured by a simple BF. These are achieved through a novel insight into the structure of graphs, namely that a graph is representable as a structured tree if and only if every loop can be wrapped around a set of connected nodes that contain at least one variable node. This condition is both necessary and sufficient. We have also explored and analyzed a specific instance of such a graph, namely a directed associative memory graph. Along with the development of the BF framework, we have implemented it as an open-source software tool available for public use. This tool enables interactive exploration of the Brief Function representation and associated queries, and is capable of handling small to medium-sized models defined over graphs. We have also evaluated its performance on a range of benchmark models, and the results show that it can handle models defined over graphs with up to a thousand variables. We conclude by discussing possible future extensions and modifications to the BF framework, along with some related open research questions. When subjected to high stresses, the vast majority of fluids undergo shear thickening, a sudden and extreme increase in resistance to flow that can often grind to a halt. Despite its surprising frequency, the underlying causes of shear thickening remain poorly understood, with different theories attributing its origin to either localized events disrupting flow or viscoelastic behavior. To gain insight into these mechanisms, our laboratory extensively examines the shear thickening transition in cornstarch mixed with water over a broad range of concentrations and temperatures. Through careful analysis of our data in relation to material properties and microscopically observed particle interactions, we reveal a universal relationship governing the onset of shear thickening that is unaffected by the specific characteristics of a particular material. Validating our found equation across multiple experiments, we demonstrate a precise match between predicted and observed shear thickening onset points. Furthermore, we delve into the entanglement mechanics of particles during shear thickening, revealing that the transition point marks the beginning of irreversible particle capture, a phenomenon that can be influenced by the shape of particles. In the course of our study, we also investigate the effects of concentration and temperature on particle interactions and microstructure, finding that changes in these parameters alter the material's microstructure in ways that directly impact the shear thickening transition. Our findings also imply that concentrated emulsions and suspensions behave similarly during shear thickening, a discovery that allows us to incorporate cross-linked polymer models into our analysis. With our findings in mind, we propose a way to distinguish between different theories of shear thickening based on the material's microstructure, and we examine the conditions necessary for shear thickening to become so severe that it becomes impossible to resume flow once the stress is removed. An area where Web search personalization's effect on professional research has been inadequately studied is the risk of experts missing relevant information caused by the bias in Google's Web search results. This study's aim is to investigate this risk among enterprise software professionals in relation to Web search for bug patterns. A combination of existing Bug Pattern Databases and Web search was used to discover the frequency of relevant information being overlooked. Specifically, it was determined how often (i) Web search fails to reveal existing bug pattern knowledge and (ii) how much additional information is missed when accounting for Google's personalization. A novel metric, the Overlooked Relevant Information Ratio (ORIR), was developed to measure this risk. A survey involving the retrieval of 2,478 bug patterns using Web search and subsequent evaluation against established Bug Pattern Databases was conducted to assess this risk. The results show that about 1 in 5 Web search queries fail to discover existing bug pattern knowledge, and that Google's personalization leads to a 25% greater risk of information being missed. Furthermore, by utilizing ORIR, the study demonstrates a way to quantify the risk of Web search personalization for various professions. In conclusion, this study highlights the importance of considering Web search's bias in research, specifically in relation to bug patterns, and suggests that its impact could be similar for other areas of research. The study's findings are relevant to anyone who uses Google's Web search, including but not limited to software professionals, academics, and business leaders. The development of ORIR provides a tool for evaluating the effect of Web search personalization on various domains, which can be utilized by a wide range of users. The study highlights the need for alternative search engines with less bias, and the development of better methods for reducing Web search bias's impact on research. The study's findings in relation to enterprise software professionals also highlight the need for more effective knowledge management systems that minimize the risk of information being overlooked due to Web search bias. The development of ORIR provides a way to quantify this risk in relation to the characteristics of Web search queries, which can be utilized by search engine designers, knowledge management system developers, and researchers. The study's findings are relevant to a wide range of areas, including software maintenance, natural language processing, and knowledge management. This conversion could provide opportunities for new physics investigations and re-deployment of existing infrastructure. We are examining the feasibility of this idea by investigating the present state of the MAMI facility's accelerator complex, identifying obstacles to its use for heavy-ion research, and exploring possible solutions to those challenges. We are also examining the potential scientific benefits of such a facility, including investigations of hadrontherapy, the study of striction, and the investigation of rare muon processes that could lead to better understanding of physics beyond the Standard Model. Although we selected the MAMI facility for analysis, we believe its replacement could be any other muon accelerator complex that is suited for this purpose. We are encouraging institutions that own or operate similar facilities to consider this idea and provide information that could aid in this kind of analysis. Data acquisition is continuous via a spiral acquisition method with reordering of Cartesian sampling points (rCASPR) that ensures minimal respiratory blurring and automatic alignment of MRI data with patient breathing cycles. A simulation study was conducted to evaluate rCASPR in various respiratory scenarios and contrast weighting conditions. Additionally, experiments were designed to test rCASPR on a pet-like phantom moving in different rhythms and on actual subjects with varying breathing patterns. The results showed that rCASPR effectively suppresses respiratory blurring and anatomical detail retention during data reconstruction. However, some residual blurring was observed in a few prctiles of the distribution of spiral sampling uniformity. In a clinical application on a human body, rCASPR demonstrated adequate spatial resolution in various T2 weighting conditions. The open nature of rCASPR allows for easy modification of the algorithm for other MRI sequences. The free acquisition protocol is suitable for various MRI platforms and provides optimal sampling patterns for low-resolution reconstruction in different respiratory periods and T2 weighting conditions. The paired-permutation test has proven effective in detecting structured deviations in the distribution of aggregated data. To efficiently carry out paired-permutation tests on data with a particular structure, such as block-diagonal or networked components, permutation operations are optimally conducted within the marginal distributions of each structured segment. However, implementing these tests can be complicated by an lack of access to the internal structure of the data. In response to this challenge, we develop a new testing method called paired-permutation examination (PPE). This novel approach pairs each data point with a different corresponding point, selected from a different dataset, as opposed to paired-permutation tests which match points with their identical counterparts. We demonstrate that the paired-permutation examination test is equivalent to the paired-permutation test in regards to its test statistic distribution. Furthermore, PPE provides a convenient yet precise way to carry out paired-permutation tests without prior knowledge of the data's internal structure. Unlike paired-permutation tests, the PPE method enables us to determine the specific segments of the data where deviations in distribution have occurred, a capability that has no equivalent in the paired-permutation test framework. In addition, PPE can be implemented using network optimization and machine learning, making it suitable for applications involving complex networks. In our analysis, we illustrate how PPE can be employed to detect falsehoods in network-based statistical models. In these examples, we show that PPE successfully identifies the incorrect components of the data where the model's distribution has been altered. In contrast, paired-permutation tests fail to provide this level of precision and accuracy in detecting structured deviations in data. In summary, the paired-permutation examination test provides a more precise and accurate way of carrying out paired-permutation tests, and as such, it has significant implications for any application that involves the paired-permutation test, including biostatistics, economics, and political science. In these fields, PPE can be used to validate the consistency of statistical models with real data, a practice that is fundamental to obtaining reliable and verifiable knowledge. In our discussion, we highlight the connections between PPE and other methods that can be used for this purpose, such as P-power and synthetic data. The fabric space $|K|$ of a simplicial complex $K$ is defined as the collection of points corresponding to vertices in $K$, together with lines representing edges and filled regions representing fillable triangles. Two key observations about $|K|$ are made. Firstly, the triangulation of any region in $|K|$ can be determined by locally reconfiguring the points, lines, and filled regions within that specific region, without affecting the triangulation of other regions. Secondly, this local reconfiguration is equivalent to a sequence of edge flips in the original complex $K$. Based on these observations, a new approach is developed for modeling the process of edge flip rearrangements within a simplex $\Delta^n$. Specifically, the space of triangulations on $\Delta^n$ is topologically encoded into a higher-dimensional complex called the n-folded cube, denoted as $\Delta^n\square\square\ldots\square$ (with n copies of the cube). The main contribution of this research is the introduction of the concept of a dynamic simplex, defined as a variant of the folded cube, specifically $\Delta^n\square\square\ldots\square$ (with n copies of the cube). The idea of a dynamic simplex is more general and allows for the encodement of any discrete process that involves the edge flip rearrangements within a simplex. The development of the dynamic simplex is also presented through the fabric space approach, with the resulting encodement of the process being inaccessible through the traditional edge flip perspective. The research in this paper is related to a broader project that aims to use the edge flip rearrangements within a simplex as the basic step in a larger process, with the goal of investigating fundamental aspects of time, geometry, and process encodement. The development of the dynamic simplex through the fabric space approach leads to the encodement of the edge flip rearrangements within a simplex as the 1-skeleton of the (n+1)-folded cube, specifically $\Delta^{n+1}\square\square\ldots\square$ (with n+1 copies of the cube). The encodement of the edge flip rearrangements within a simplex as the 1-skeleton of the (n+1)-folded cube can be interpreted in three distinct ways, representing either the triangulation of a triangle in a recursive manner, the result of applying the process of edge flip rearrangements within a triangle, or the topological space of triangulations of a triangle. We investigated the drag experienced by a cylindrical object moving through a layer of granular material, specifically focusing on the effect of orientation and whether the grains are loose or compacted. This study considered a two-dimensional model where the cylindrical object moves through a layer of granular material, both on a flat surface and saturated with a fluid. By analyzing the drag force on the cylinder as it moves, we found that the orientation of the cylinder affects the drag force, with the maximum force encountered when it is moved at a 45-degree angle. Furthermore, this research showed that the drag force increases more significantly in loose granular materials than in compacted materials. Additionally, the change in orientation was found to influence the fluid flow around the cylinder, with the wake flow changing from turbulent to laminar as the cylinder is rotated from 0 to 90 degrees. This shift from turbulent to laminar flow as the orientation changes was linked to the formation of longitudinal vortices in the direction of motion. This happens when the cylinder is moved at a 90-degree angle, resulting in the drag force becoming independent of the fluid flow. This finding is particularly significant because it demonstrates that the drag force on an object in a fluid-saturated granular medium can be determined by analyzing the grain dynamics alone, without considering the fluid flow. This is similar to the behavior observed in dry granular media, where the drag force becomes independent of the orientation when the cylinder is moved at a 90-degree angle. This research also examined the effect of surface roughness on the drag force and found that it increases with greater roughness, especially in loose granular materials. This increase in drag force due to surface roughness was found to be more significant when the cylinder is moved at a 45-degree angle. This study further explored the drag force in saturated conditions and found that it can be determined using the approach developed, even when the granular material is initially loose. This is because the drag force becomes independent of the orientation as long as the average stress in the granular material remains constant. This finding is linked to the behavior observed in dry granular media, where the drag force becomes independent of the orientation when the cylinder is moved at a 90-degree angle. A critical aspect in devising numerical methods for time-dependent partial differential equations involves preserving inherent properties of the original solution. Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing preservation-based discretization techniques, including validating existing algorithms' preservation properties and proposing innovative methods achieving high accuracy while maintaining property preservation. Both of these endeavors are  necessary for ensuring the validity of simulations based on these methods. Although such schemes, when combined with efficient time-stepping methods like the Krylov subspace reduction, have significant practical applications, there's a noticeable lack of studies on the preservation properties of these combined schemes. This paper addresses this gap by investigating the preservation of a specific property - addition preservation - in combined schemes involving Krylov methods. Specifically, we discuss both Krylov algorithms and combined schemes' preservation properties, highlighting the importance of viable options like flexible Krylov methods, and providing novel proofs for the preservation of a given property in combined schemes. Moreover, we introduce flexible Krylov-based versions of existing preservation-based time-stepping methods and both numerically and graphically verify the validity of these combined schemes through simulations based on various models. One of these models includes the nonlinear Schrödinger equation. In addition, we outline a strategy for developing combined schemes ensuring preservation properties, ending with a discussion on the open problems presented in this paper. Finally, we offer a bibliography of related studies on the subject. This paper is dedicated to the memory of its second author, the esteemed Professor Chris Tisdell. Due to the limited scope of this study, we only considered the preservation of the identity $u(n)=e^{n}u(0)$, and recommend exploring the preservation of other important properties in combined schemes, such as multiplicative preservation, additive preservation, and Hamiltonian preservation. We also suggest investigating the convergence of flexible Krylov-based schemes and the application of these schemes to Hamiltonian partial differential equations. Furthermore, we believe that both theoretical and numerical analyses are necessary to establish the accuracy and stability of these schemes. We intend to investigate these aspects in our future work. Determining scene flow involves calculating the three-dimensional motion trajectories for specific points within an animated three-dimensional environment. Motion trajectory data has been found beneficial for downstream tasks like activity classification and object segmentation. Nonetheless, obtaining precise data through laser scanning and stereo imaging is cumbersome and time-consuming. Consequently, training networks with abundant supervised data remains a preferable alternative. We present a novel method called Self-Guided Scene Flow Network (SGF-Net) that learns from intrinsic metrics without relying on ground truth data, thereby making it suitable for practical applications in dynamic real-world environments. Unlike traditional metric learning models, SGF-Net leverages adversarial training to obtain a distinctive distribution of optical flow estimates, which in turn facilitates efficient scene flow estimation. We validate the (SGF-Net) model on extensive dynamic datasets and observe its superior performance in comparison to conventional methods. Moreover, we analyze the functional components of SF-Net through a visual explanation of its flow trajectory reconstruction capability. Finally, we demonstrate the practical utility of SF-Net in complex real-world settings, including outdoor motion tracking and indoor activity classification. The associated code has been publicly released on GitHub at https://github.com/ChengxiangCao/Self-Guided-Scene-Flow-Network.

This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call policy learning in containerized microservices. During operation, Timeloops automatically isolates specific sub-components of an application, on a per-request basis, using system call privileges. These sub-components, called Timeloops modules, are then evaluated for efficiency and security by testing them individually with controlled samples of real operation data. These tests are used to create a record of system call privileges for each module, which are then combined to create a policy for the full application. Our study shows that, when applying Timeloops to real-world applications, it is possible to reduce system call privileges and minimize performance losses of around 12%. Furthermore, when incorporating security testing into the framework, it is possible to discover and fix security vulnerabilities in popular open-source applications, which otherwise would have been discovered through scanning tools. Our findings also highlight that Timeloops modules often overlap, which can be simplified by consolidating identical modules, reducing the number of system call privileges and resulting performance gains of up to 21%. Our research further discovers that containers often grant too many system call privileges, with an average of 37% of privileges being unnecessary. Our results demonstrate that in addition to security and efficiency, Timeloops can also provide better system call privilege reduction, which can be achieved by deploying Timelolops in development environments. Our data shows that it is possible to deploy large-scale applications securely with minimal system call privileges, with an analysis of system call privilege usage revealing that it complies with established security standards. Our research highlights various obstacles that prevent widespread adoption of Timeloops, which could provide developmental support for securing and optimizing system call privileges in containers. Our findings suggest that although Timeloops is capable of reducing system call privileges in development environments, it is limited to static analysis and cannot handle complex, dynamic applications that involve multiple Timeloops modules interacting with each other. Our study also discovers that in addition to system call privileges, other developmental obstacles, which are unrelated to Timeloops, significantly hinder the adoption of secure and efficient system call privileges in containers. A distinctive and widespread neural development pattern called interkinetic nuclear migration (IKNM) is observed in vertebrate forebrains. It involves the back-and-forth movement of cell nuclei between the upper and lower boundaries of neuroblast layers as new neurons are generated. While the processes and mechanisms driving this pattern of movement are not well understood, studies have shown that restricting cell movement can halt neurogenesis, indicating a crucial role for IKNM in brain development. However, the specific developmental importance of cell nucleus movement patterns remains unclear. Using high-speed lighting to observe IKNM in developing zebrafish retina, our findings reveal that rather than following a directed course, cell nucleus movements appear random and diffuse, failing to exhibit the linear trajectory typically observed in this pattern. Our further analysis of these movements, using elements of stochastic theory, demonstrate that retinal IKNM can be explained by a combination of retinal expansion and cell nucleus diffusion. Our results also show that the anucleate neural progenitor cells, which contribute to the retina, exhibit a different migration pattern compared to bipolar cell progenitors, which contribute to the neuroblast layer. Interestingly, the finding that anucleate neural progenitor cells exhibit a linear migration pattern, in contrast to the diffuse migration observed in bipolar cell progenitors, provides a potentially critical explanation for the structural development of the retina. Furthermore, our findings highlight the utility of stochastic analysis in understanding the mechanisms governing IKNM, and the retail retina as a model system for studying this phenomenon. In this study, we provide improved code options for two image processing problems: compressive video retrieval with coded apertures and color image demosaicing with coded apertures. Originally proposed coded apertures utilize coding theory to reduce data by limiting the capture to a subset of encoded apertures, and both of these applications benefit from this technique by reducing the amount of data needed for efficient retrieval or image reconstruction. We introduce two new coded apertures: one with complementary pairs that significantly boosts the retrieval performance by up to 6dB in certain cases, and a pseudo-random coded aperture that greatly simplifies the coded aperture design while still reducing data by 40% with a minimal performance degradation. We also make the code options more versatile by providing algorithms for adjusting the coded apertures during the processing stage. All of the proposed coded apertures are simple, efficient designs with a focus on balancing low data rates and high image quality. They can be applied to a broad range of image and video processing tasks beyond just compressive video retrieval and color image demosaicing. We show that any countable group of diffeomorphisms from a compact surface to itself is precompact within the space of continuous functions from the surface to itself, when the topology is defined by a system of local scales that excludes excessively large scales. This precompactness is not dependent on whether the group in question is generated by orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms or not. Additionally, we establish that any group that is generated by orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms and satisfies certain bonding properties is locally compact. These results extend and modify previous outcomes by Krylov and Neumann for 2-dimensional surfaces and by Gaifullin for surfaces of higher dimensions. The novel approach introduced in this study also enables us to demonstrate that certain specific groups, such as the monodromies of hyperbolic surfaces and surface mapping class groups, are precompact. This research also discusses related topics, including the absence of compact subgroups generated by orientation-reversing diffeomorphisms and the surface group's solvability within the space of continuous functions. Lastly, we provide an appendix on the relation between local scale space and the Roelcke topology.

For isotropic systems consisting of randomly arranged particles, the average effect of coexisting particles with different characteristics (whether they attract each other or repel each other in multiple dimensions) depends solely on the average characteristics of those particles. However, when considering a 2D Ising-like system with coexisting particles that can have n-dimensional characteristics, the average effect of those particles isn't simply the average of those characteristics. Instead, the average effect is influenced by the specific coexistence conditions and can switch from a tendency to align to a tendency to ignore each other, even in the absence of any dimensionality n. This behavior is observed for any odd value of n greater than 1. This system's sensitivity to the coexisting particles' characteristics means that changing those characteristics can lead to a range of different average effects, making it challenging to predict the average effect of unseen coexisting particles. This complexity becomes particularly pronounced when considering systems with multiple order parameters. This finding is relevant to existing research models and provides a new physical example of a system with multiple coexisting phases that exhibit hysteresis due to random fluctuations. This example can also be realized in both magnetic and liquid state systems. This system's complexity also allows for multiple possible scenario combinations that could arise, some of which are depicted in the paper's figures. We validated our method on a simulation involving a Point Mass model with dynamic obstacles. The results showed that our approach yields accurate estimates of the second-order achievable sets while outperforming the first-order method and achieving a balance between the precision of the estimates and the computation time. The research also emphasized the potential applications of the Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equations in various contexts, such as robotic motion planning, feedback stabilization, and game theory. By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to unfamiliar tasks without explicit guidance, humans demonstrate impressive cross-task capabilities.
This study aims to enhance the cross-task generalization ability of massive language models in unsupervised settings, with a focus on models like T0 and FLAN.
We introduce a novel, unsupervised retrieval-based method known as ReCross, which employs inactive tasks to facilitate a more precise representation of inclusive data distributions.
By incorporating a diverse range of tasks that can help models better distinguish between similar data points and enhance their intrinsic inductive capabilities, ReCross significantly boosts the efficacy of current models in evaluating cross-task generalization.
Our proposed method shines in particular in scenarios where evaluation datasets are heavily balanced, inconsistent, or heavily skewed towards minority classes.
Through carefully designed experiments, we validate the effectiveness of ReCross across various balanced and imbalanced cross-task generalization settings, revealing its potential to handle diverse evaluation scenarios with ease.
By releasing our code and models, we hope to inspire further improvements and provide a platform for investigating other unsupervised cross-task generalization methods. 
With over 40% improvement seen in certain challenging scenarios, ReCross stands to improve the cross-task generalization of state-of-the-art language models. 
Our findings are supported by extensive evaluation frameworks, involving rigorous tests of large-language-models on both JFLL and HANS.

By simply employing a diverse set of tasks, we successfully induced 25% to 50% reductions in errors made by models in various setting, further solidifying the benefits of diverse task training. 
In a notable experiment, our method was applied to a real-world scenario involving customer service conversations, yielding striking 13% to 25% improvements when evaluating models on unfamiliar queries.

Differentially private deep learning has seen significant growth, and a key challenge is optimizing the tuning of hyperparameters, learning rate schedules, and model architecture. We have discovered that, similar to non-private methods, better results can be achieved with state-of-the-art hyperparameter optimization techniques. However, existing differentially private methods lack structured methods for tuning hyperparameters, learning rate schedules, and models, compared to their non-private counterparts. We introduced a new hyperparameter optimization framework based on the application of the Exponential Mechanism, which provides a principled approach to tuning hyperparameters, learning rate schedules, and models in a private setting. We also developed a software tool called Private Tuner to facilitate this process, showcasing the effectiveness of our approach with a range of experiments using robust stochastic gradient descent, adversarial training, and federated learning. Our results demonstrate significant improvements in differentially private deep learning performance. The code for Private Tuner is available at https://github.com/ghrasoul/Private-Tuner. We published this work at the IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR) 2023, where it can be found in full detail.

A novel approach to measuring the distance to galaxies has been discovered by examining planetary nebulae with similar spectral properties, which share a correlated absorption in their spectra. This indicator, known as PNeSe, is characterized by a specific combination of [O III] and [N II] emission, distinguishing 10-20% of planetary nebulae spectra. A automatic method was developed to measure the PNeSe parameter, which enabled a precise determination of the distance to galaxies in the Fornax cluster through a constant planetary nebula luminosity function. A preliminary analysis of 1450 planetary nebulae spectra gathered from 105 galaxies yielded a mean PNeSe parameter of 1.557 ± 0.005, consistent with other measurements of the distance to the Fornax cluster. By utilizing a modified version of the PNeSe method, an independent validation was performed using individual planetary nebulae with known distances, resulting in a mean distance error of 7.5%. A comparative study of other methods to measure the distance to galaxies in the Fornax cluster cluster using planetary nebulae as standard candles found that the PNeSe method yields the most precise results, with a mean distance error of 5.6%. The widespread occurrence of PNeSe in galaxy spectra, coupled with its ease of measurement, makes this method an attractive and highly reliable way to measure the distance to galaxies using planetary nebulae as standard candles. The comprehensive data set of planetary nebulae spectra and corresponding PNeSe parameters for the Fornax cluster galaxies is available for further study. The data and methodology used for this research are available upon request. Every day, hospitals around the world gather vast amounts of physiological data from their patients, leading to an escalating interest in conducting statistical analyses to provide better medical diagnoses. These analyses involve complex computations on significant datasets, necessitating high-performance data processing systems that can balance efficiency and simplicity. To address the limitations of existing stream processing engines for periodic streams, we present Streams for Life (LifeStream), a lightweight engine specifically designed to efficiently process periodic flows by combining two processing models: continuous and micro-batch. LifeStream optimizes performance while preserving the ease of implementation afforded by continuous processing, and our evaluations using real-data from an electrocardiography application demonstrate that LifeStream achieves a 50% reduction in execution time compared to a leading stream processing engine. Moreover, LifeStream's efficient design enables a 2.5 times performance boost in limited memory configurations. Our research highlights that, with careful design, efficient and simple periodic stream processing can be achieved, paving the way for its practical use in various domains. Our contribution takes the form of a reusable, open-source framework available under the Apache License, capable of stream processing, combined batch-stream execution, and persistent storage of temporary data.

This research paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically those in higher dimensional space, do not fit the classification of Bertrand curves except in two-dimensional Euclidean space. A new category, called the timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curve, is defined to fill this gap and its characteristics are identified for curves in a four-dimensional space. Specifically, the conditions are established for a curve to be considered a timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curve in a semi-Riemannian three-dimensional space of signature (1,3). Furthermore, key properties of these curves are proven, including that they lie on a surface defined by a particular second-order differential equation, and that they have a unique characteristic curve associated with them. The relationship between these curves and the geodesics of a specific surface of revolution is also established. Finally, the paper concludes by examining the (1,3)-Bertrand curve in the context of a four-dimensional space and presenting an example of a timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curve in a semi-Riemannian space of signature (3,3).

Re-training a neural network with a new loss function is thought to require re-initializing the neural network, due to the significant impact of the early layers being sensitive to the input data. This conviction has been a cornerstone of machine learning theory since the early days of neural networks. However, this study aims to explore the degree to which this principle holds true in deep learning. We designed an experiment where we trained a ResNet-50 on one dataset and applied it to a different dataset, and then re-trained the model using a soft-plus loss function with data augmentation. We found that only a 0.01 change occurred in the weights of the early layers, despite the loss function being significantly modified. We also discovered that the primary source of influence is limited to the last layer, which is the softmax layer. We believe that this study's findings deserve broader attention in the machine learning community. Additionally, we observed that the soft-plus loss function's impact was analogous to using a probability distribution other than categorical, and that the influence of the loss function's modification could be mitigated by re-training the last layer alone. We achieved this by re-training the last layer of a pre-trained ResNet-50 on one dataset, and then applying it to a different dataset, and the results showed a 7% improvement in accuracy. We also explored other loss functions such as logistic loss, focal loss, and AM-L1 loss, and found that our approach's effectiveness was loss-function-agnostic. We concluded that this approach's effectiveness could be attributed to the degree of the last layer's over-confidence, and that we could further improve the results by applying techniques that reduce over-confidence. Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday common knowledge reasoning rules comprised of nearly 280,000 text-based descriptions.  This atlas of dialogues, represented as causal relationships between actors and their surroundings, is organized around a central concept of agency.  We demonstrate that by employing a two-part framework where a natural language processing component generates causes and effects from text, a rule-based system can effectively produce reasonable responses based on community-derived standards.  Our findings show that even without training, a simple model can effectively determine the cause and effect of a given description by relying on general language properties.  Furthermore, by analyzing the complex interactions within ATOMIC, we uncover subtle aspects of agency, demonstrating that simple models can distort basic elements of the data.  Our proposed dataset and analysis tools are available at \url{http://atomic.data}.

One of the most compelling applications of quantum computing lies in its ability to accelerate linear algebraic problems through iterative linear solvers, particularly the use of the Quantum Linear Algebra Package (QLAP). QLAP includes operations for solving linear systems, transforming matrices, and evaluating matrix functions. Building upon the QLAP framework, we've developed the Quantum Integrated Matrix Package (QIMP), a comprehensive quantum package that incorporates additional capabilities such as the ability to solve multi-system linear systems, perform matrix exponentiation, and calculate the matrix logarithm. QIMP represents a significant advancement over the QLAP package and showcases the potential for its portfolio of algorithms. Moreover, these algorithms can be combined to achieve even more complex quantum operations, demonstrating the promise of integrated quantum packages in tackling real-world challenges. In contrast to the QLAP, the QIMP package uses the HHL algorithm as its base, although both packages are compatible with each other. The development of the QIMP package serves as an illustration of the HHL algorithm's implementation, which can be challenging due to its intricate requirements, including the need for efficient error control, sufficient quantum memory, and the HHL algorithm's prolonged execution time. The QIMP source code is available on GitHub, presenting a practical example of an integrated quantum package that can be applied to real-world applications. The matrix polynomial transformation's implementation marks the first time this capability is available on a quantum device, further demonstrating the HHL algorithm's effectiveness in combining multiple matrix operations, including the matrix polynomial evaluation and the matrix logarithm, which can be combined to achieve the matrix exponential evaluation, among other operations. The development of the QIMP package and the HHL algorithm-based solutions were tested on the IBM Quantum Hardware, specifically the ibmq_boeing chip, which allowed for the comparison of the quantum execution against classical simulation, resulting in execution times of up to 4592.11 ms and an error rate of 89\%. To enhance speech recognition using state-of-the-art transformers, we propose a new method that expands training on transformer-based models to incorporate text and speech inputs in a speech-text oriented manner. This approach leads to a more comprehensive understanding of speech and text by capturing their interdependencies and has two key effects: it broadens the attention within the transformer encoder and allows for the creation of a multi-headed encoder that combines speech and text attention. We introduce a bidirectional focus mechanism to make full use of both speech and text information and our experiments demonstrate substantial gains in WER on both Librispeech and Switchboard datasets. Specifically, with a batch size of 80, our model achieves 5.5% WER on the Librispeech "easy" set and 6.4% WER on the Switchboard dataset. Our findings also highlight the importance of properly tuning the hyperparameters, particularly the ratio of speech to text masking, in order to avoid performance degradation. Our code has been made available at https://github.com/Paralel/SpeechTextTransformer.

Measurements of superconducting nanowires, particularly NbN nanowires, indicate the presence of a critical voltage threshold below which conductivity is inhibited due to the accumulation of charge or phase slips. The behavior of an all-solid-state quantum circuit comprising a single superconducting nanowire connected to a gate electrode and an ohmic load was investigated. By applying a large DC current through the gate, we observed that the conductivity threshold vanished, and the conductance became uniform. This consequence can be explained by either the suppression of the coherent phase slips that maintain a multiple of the quanta of phase, or the formation of a Coulomb blockade barrier, depending on the condition. The possibility of both situations exists, though we prefer the phase slip hypothesis as the primary mechanism. The possibility of the Coulomb blockade scenario is supported by the low-temperature measurements that indicate the presence of a small conductance gap within the conductance curve. Furthermore, we found that increasing the capacitance of the gate electrode led to a rise in the conductivity threshold, which could be anticipated from the phase slip hypothesis. The possibility of the charge obstruction scenario is less likely in this situation. The influence of the gate electrode's capacitance was also tested by applying a small AC signal to the gate, which resulted in the conductivity threshold varying with the DC component of the gate voltage. The measurements can be explained by the motion of a single discrete phase slip state. The study has implications for the use of nanowires in quantum circuits and emphasizes the significance of considering the influence of the environment on the capacitance of the nanowires. In applications such as video surveillance and remote operations, view video forecasting can be very useful by predicting the view of a situation or an object from a different camera angle than is currently being observed. In this research, a novel approach is taken to forecast the view video in a specific scenario, with two distinct representations used to capture movement and density changes in the video. A dense connection is employed to combine two simple convolutional neural networks, each processing different resolution images of the same scene. This combined representation is then utilized to forecast the view video in a different camera angle. To test this innovation, an innovative dataset called NYP was created, consisting of negative camera view videos recorded in normal daily activities during the COVID-19 pandemic. Experimental results showed that this approach yields superior outcomes when compared to state-of-the-art methods in both evaluation metrics. Airborne transmission of diseases in confined spaces is a significant concern, and the level of mixing assumed in epidemiological models can substantially impact their precision. This study examines the accuracy of partially and fully mixed models in predicting COVID-19 transmission on urban buses. Utilizing a numerical method that accounts for individual respiratory patterns, particle transport, and the effects of viral droplets, we simulated various scenarios of transmission. Our findings show that both partially and fully mixed models can effectively approximate the spread of illness, although a fully mixed model generally performs better. A key observation from this study involves identifying the minimum level of breathing rate required to accurately represent bus transmission dynamics using a fully mixed model. Furthermore, we found that the level of mixing can switch during the course of a bus journey, potentially affecting the accuracy of results. A simple model is introduced to assess this phenomenon, along with suggestions for future research to further engage with this complex issue. Overall, this study highlights the importance of precise level of mixing in models used to forecast disease transmission in urban buses, along with potential avenues for future research to be explored. Our research was previously published in the journal Scientific Reports, under the title ``Quantifying breathing patterns to predict COVID-19 transmission on urban buses'' along with a related correction titled ``Correction: Quantifying breathing patterns to predict COVID-19 transmission on urban buses''. We demonstrate the efficacy of this strategy by conducting experiments on several classification tasks, and show that it outperforms existing methods in various settings. Our approach and findings are applicable to neural networks, including those used for reinforcement learning, and our code is available at: https://github.com/ghruan/Lipschitz-regularization.

The beam disruption instability issue is a critical challenge in energy recovery linacs, where a low-intensity beam is overlapped with the strong wakefields generated by a high-intensity beam traveling in the same accelerator section. Studies have shown that the filling configuration significantly affects beam disruption instability and that properly designed fill configurations can minimize this instability. However, the complex interplay between coherent radiation, beam bunches, and scatterers introduces an additional variable that affects beam disruption instability. This study examines how the orientation of beam polarization influences coherent radiation and thus affects beam disruption instability, and it demonstrates that carefully selecting the beam polarization orientation can further reduce this instability. Furthermore, this study explores various filling configurations that incorporate beam bunches oriented at different angles and shows that correctly chosen configurations can reduce beam disruption instability by as much as a factor of ten. This finding suggests that careful consideration of beam polarization is a straightforward and effective approach to managing beam disruption instability in energy recovery linacs. This research was conducted using both numerical analysis and particle simulation tools and has been applied to the Advanced Proton Source energy recovery linac, where it demonstrated a comparable level of performance improvement. This study's results are relevant to other energy recovery linacs that utilize ring configurations and could be adapted for those systems with similar design features. This study's findings on beam polarization-oriented scattering to reduce beam disruption instability have also been confirmed through comparative analysis of different scattering orientations. We conducted a search for binary asteroids within Pan-STARRS1 images by applying a set of criteria to photometric, astrometric, and characteristic properties.  We utilized surveys including the Pan-STARRS1, Sloan Digital Sky Survey, and Two-color All Sky Survey to identify and characterize potential binary asteroids and distinguish them from misleading objects such as star binaries, comets, satellites, asteroids with unusual shapes, or meteors.  Our analysis resulted in an estimated 0.4% to 1.4% binary asteroid ratio among main asteroid belt asteroids with diameters exceeding 100 km, which is substantially lower than predicted ratios based on numerical simulations and observational findings regarding near-Earth asteroids.  We found that the binary asteroid ratio among Kirkwood gap asteroids is dramatically low, likely linked to disruption by mean motion resonances.  Our study indicates that binaries among the larger main belt asteroids prefer circular orbits, with eccentricities less than 0.3, and also prefer low-inclination orbits.  We discovered a binary asteroid candidate with a marked infrared emission pattern, suggesting it has a rocky composition similar to that of 4 Vesta and 10 Hygiea.  Our findings were compared to previous research involving binary asteroids found by the Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph and the Hubble Space Telescope, utilizing similar criteria to identify overlapping targets.  Among these, we found candidates for further study using higher resolution and spectroscopic data, including targets such as the asteroid (6) Hebe, which is a rocky asteroid with a highly irregular shape and an uncertain composition.  Our analysis resulted in an estimated binary asteroid ratio among small main belt asteroids with diameters less than 100 km of 5.0% to 10.0%, which is consistent with predictions based on numerical simulations and findings from comprehensive simulations involving impact break-up.  Our study highlights the distinctive characteristics of binary asteroids within this size group, including flat inclinations and circular orbits.  We conclude that searching historical images is an effective way to discover binary asteroids, providing a practical solution for future large-scale surveys involving high-magnification observations.  Finally, we discuss the limitations of this research due to the limited resolution of Pan-STARRS1 images and the small size of discovered targets, which prevents the detection of exponents greater than 10 km and binary asteroids with closely spaced orbits.  The resulting binary asteroid database is available online, featuring 141 confirmed binary asteroids discovered within Pan-STARRS1 images.  This research was supported by the National Astr

Recently, research has focused on the analysis of linear regression models involving network data, especially with respect to covariates that follow a Gaussian distribution. However, there is a need for studies on the estimation of linear regression models using electronic health records, which often feature right-skewed covariates. We have developed statistical methods to identify a partially linear regression model involving a network-based covariate and provide evidence of our approach's effectiveness in a setting with peer influences. Our research utilizes a hospital data set comprising 35,514 patients across 346 hospitals and demonstrates that our method correctly estimates the partially linear regression coefficients and functions. Moreover, we have analyzed network peer influences by incorporating a measure of hospital network structure and several covariates, and have found that the extent of peer influence varies significantly across different hospitals and that the degree of peer influence is associated with a hospital's specific characteristics, such as its bed count, a measure of malpractice litigation in the surrounding area, and the presence of particular medical specialties. Our findings suggest that the distribution of a hospital's network, namely how its hospitals are connected, exerts a more substantial influence on a hospital's peer influence than the distribution of its covariates, which can be seen as indicating that peer influences are sensitive to changes in hospital network structure rather than covariates. We have also investigated how peer influences shape outcomes in hospitals and found that the positive or negative effects of peer influences on a hospital's outcome are influenced by the degree of randomness present in the distribution of a hospital's network. If the network is random then peer influences either have a positive effect on outcomes or do not affect them, whereas in a structured network peer influences either do not affect outcomes or have a negative effect on them. Our research highlights the importance of taking into account a hospital's network structure and the randomness present in this structure when measuring peer influences and outcomes in hospitals. We have analyzed the robustness of our methods by conducting a simulation study and found that our approaches are highly reliable and consistent with the true values of the parameters being estimated. We have further tested the applicability of our methods to models with non-parametric components and to models with parametric components, and to models with both parametric and non-parametric components, and to models with linear random effects. Our research provides theoretical evidence of the asymptotic consistency and normality of the estimated parameters, and we have investigated the finite sample properties of our methods using a simulation study. This study introduces novel versions of the Riemann-Liouville variable-order fractional integral and derivative, and we prove a modified Leibniz rule applies to these operators. Specifically, we establish that the proportionality constant can be variables that depend on the limit of integration. By utilizing these definitions within the context of the variable-order fractional derivative, we demonstrate that they lead to new versions of the Leibniz rule, offering potential uses in solving and studying the properties of fractional differential equations. Furthermore, we establish a connection between our new definition and existing ones, showing it can be viewed as a type of Leibniz rule context. Additionally, we derive a key theorem related to the composition of these operators, and provide examples of variable-order fractional derivatives for specific functions. Lastly, we discuss our findings and existing research on the subject matter. We introduce the GPT-3 based model, AI Dungeon Master, which engages in conversations with players in Dungeons and Dragons tournaments. By analyzing the intentions behind player actions, the model determines their goals, identifying both explicit (e.g. killing a monster) and implicit ones (e.g. conserving magic spells). In this process, it develops a theory of mind that reflects the relationships between players, their motivations, and how they perceive each other. Through the model's interactions with solo players and in group settings, our research reveals how player motivations influence their behavior and provide a framework for categorizing intentions. Furthermore, our findings highlight how the model's theory of mind changes in response to changes in the game world, paving the way for future applications in evaluating large language model dialogue systems. The intricate relationship between protein knots and their spatial arrangements is an area that topological and structural biology are jointly exploring. To uncover the underlying pattern, our research employed recent advanced topological techniques to analyze the 3D structures of protein knots, focusing on the specific shape element known as a Hopf link. By investigating 194 non-homologous protein samples, our topological analysis uncovered a prominent association between Hopf links and specific protein bends, revealing that they preferentially occur in loops that are far apart. To further understand this relationship, we developed a statistical model that can distinguish genuine Hopf links from false positives, and applied it to identify the true occurrence frequency of Hopf links in protein structures. The results show that the false positive frequency can be as high as 90%, highlighting the significance of a precise definition based on actual space dimensions. By integrating this information with existing data on protein folds, our research suggests that the majority of protein folds that incorporate a Hopf link belong to a specific and distinct class, characterized by a particular loop arrangement. Consequently, we found that the occurrence of Hopf links is relatively rare, accounting for less than 0.5% of all possible protein folds that incorporate a knot. Moreover, our results indicate that the majority of protein knots are composed of a single loop, and that the majority of protein bends that resemble a Hopf link actually belong to a different topological category known as a linking of two loops that are closely bound together. The development of a statistical model to analyze the distribution of loop bonds also enabled us to create a rough metric that can quantify the complexity of a protein knot, simply referred to as its "average loop distance". The findings of this research are applicable to the study of knotted proteins, and the methods used here can be applied to the analysis of complex spatial arrangements in various fields. The availability of open-source code and additional data on protein structures and folds facilitates further research and allows for the reproduction of these results. The advanced analysis of these complex spatial arrangements also enabled us to create a realistic simulation of protein knot formation, and the code for this model has been made publicly available. A detailed investigation of a specific Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem, which deviates from its conventional form, is conducted. This particular NG theorem, associated with the symmetry breaking of a complex scalar field undergoing a non-relativistic Lorentz transformation, was initially identified in a relativistic quantum field theory context by Higashitani et al. Our analysis extends this finding to a two-dimensional space where the symmetry breaking occurs in a non-relativistic Lorentz transformation. A comparison with a one-dimensional space case is also performed to demonstrate the effects of spatial dimensions on the theorem's behavior. A key aspect of this investigation lies in the examination of the NG theorem's implications when applied to a two-dimensional space with both massless and massive scalar fields. Furthermore, the paper's conclusions are drawn by considering a $O(3)$ symmetry breaking scenario in a two-dimensional space. While counterfactual reasoning is increasingly critical in numerous applications, such as policy development, game analysis, and conversation generation, systematically constructing counterfactuals expressing "what if" a specific phrase had been different, remains a challenging task. This issue is compounded by the fact that many situations involve multiple varying elements, making it difficult to identify which aspects are key to counterfactual construction. In this paper, we introduce a novel counterfactual data generation task called phrasal counterfactual construction, where given a sentence, a relevant phrase is identified and modified to create a counterfactual. We have also created a large counterfactual dataset combining text from the Counterfactual Reasoning Challenge and the Counterfactual Machine Translation Dataset via a fusion strategy. We have tested different approaches to counterfactual construction and evaluated them using our newly developed precision and effectiveness metrics. Our results show that a strong transformer-based language model can successfully create high-quality counterfactuals when tasked with phrasal counterfactual construction, but we have also introduced a more challenging version of the task that yields less satisfactory results. We have made our datasets and implementation available to the public.

The epitaxial growth of thin films on low-energy substrates like graphene is gaining significance. It offers minimal defect introduction and allows for the formation of superlattices with novel properties. However, controlling the equilibrium between remote, pinhole, and van der Waals epitaxy on graphene substrates remains a challenge. It is influenced by factors such as film growth methods, temperature, and pressure, which affect the epitaxy equilibrium. In this study, we demonstrate the coexistence of molybdenum disulfide flakes with van der Waals epitaxy on graphene and the remote epitaxy on the sapphire substrate beneath the graphene layer. It was achieved during film deposition via molecular beam epitaxy. We observed that the film's morphology changes from remote to van der Waals epitaxy as the substrate temperature increases from 850 nm to 5 nm. It indicates that the equilibrium can be shifted by changing the kinetic energy of the precursor molecules. This finding is crucial for scaling up the remote epitaxy on complex targets with van der Waals surfaces. Furthermore, we found that the equilibrium can be stabilized in a specific state by using a molecular precursor that binds tightly with the substrate. It allows for van der Waals epitaxy on graphene over large areas, while allowing for remote epitaxy on complex substrates with small pinholes. It also enables the formation of sharp interfaces between films grown via remote and van der Waals epitaxy. This research has implications for developing superlattice structures with combined remote and van der Waals epitaxy, and demonstrates that the epitaxy equilibrium can be controlled through molecular beam epitaxy. It paves the way for scaling up the fabrication of such superlattice structures. This study also sheds light on the mechanisms of film growth on van der Waals surfaces and provides a framework for developing strategies to control the epitaxy equilibrium. It allows for the fabrication of nanostructures with designed properties and offers promising applications in quantum technologies and nanophotonics. This research has been theoretically modeled to predict the film's morphology changes in different growth conditions. It has been compared to experimental results, and demonstrates that the mechanisms of film growth on van der Waals surfaces are complex and depend on various factors such as film growth methods, temperature, and pressure. It was achieved by developing a multi-scale simulation framework that combines the mechanisms of film growth on van der Waals surfaces, the epitaxy equilibrium, the film's morphology, and the interface between films grown via remote and van der Waals epitaxy. A code is referred to as $ \Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear if it results from a particular type of encoding process called the Gray image of a code that has properties derived from $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-additive code, given a prime number p greater than two. This paper delves into the examination of the dimension of these $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes, presenting a bound on its size and demonstrating how the dimension of a code is determined by the null space of a specific generator matrix. Moreover, this matrix can be constructed from the parity-check matrix of the code, and we establish a connection between the dimension and the number of p's in the code's symbol combinations. Additionally, we provide a criterion for a code to have the maximum dimension, comprising a test that can be applied to the generator matrix or the parity-check matrix. This test enables us to determine the size of the code, or alternatively, to identify a maximum code, from which a code with the maximum size can be derived by applying Gray mapping to its elements. This paper also incorporates an illustrative example of a code with a particular structure, referred to as the direct sum code, showing how it transitions from a specific $\Z_3 \Z_9$-linear code to a code with the maximum size, following a particular encoding process. Finally, we establish a relationship between the $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes and the codes with the same parameters that are generated through the Gray mapping of the Boolean codes, proposing a potential path for future investigation. This work is an extension of a previous paper that was dedicated to the analysis of codes with the parameter p=3, and it provides several novel contributions to the field of code design and cryptography. The author also explores some specific examples that demonstrate how the $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes can be applied in various situations, concluding with an appendix that contains the background information on the codes with the parameter p=3. The paper that this abstract is based on was originally published in the European Transactions on Telecommunications.
