Conditional GANs have demonstrated superior performance in tasks requiring data balancing and an auxiliary multi-label classification task. However, these models require training on balanced data sets, which can be difficult to acquire. This paper investigates the potential of training conditional GANs on single-positive data sets, assuming each sample contains a distinct active class. An intuitive approach to apply this is in the domain of multi-class problems, where a default positive class exists for every sample, and we aim to extract instances based on their corresponding active classes. Existing methods tend to overlook the multi-label aspect and focus instead on selecting distinct instances, often resulting in labeled data sets that are inconsistent. We propose Multi-Label Unfolding Network (MLUN), a novel framework that generates high-quality multi-label instances and matches the performance of state-of-the-art methods on benchmark data sets. MLUN demonstrates its versatility in multiple applications, including semi-supervised multi-label classification and data balancing in conditional GANs. This approach offers a straightforward and effective means of preparing balanced data sets and solving multi-label classification problems using single-positive samples. Experimental evaluations validate the superior performance of MLUN in various tasks. The code for MLUN is publicly available online at https://github.com/zwang-cs/MLUN.

The GNS construction forms a correspondence between abstract C*-algebras and their associated Hilbert spaces, incorporating both algebraic structure and positive linear functionals. Contrarily, the Toeplitz-Hilbert space construction generates a C*-algegebra from a given Hilbert space and its associated positive linear operators. These two processes are inversely connected; combining the GNS construction with the Toeplitz-Hilbert space construction returns the original C*-algebra with its original set of positive linear functionals. This bilateral connection is reflected in their abstract frameworks, classified at a 2-Categorical level, where the GNS construction forms a right adjoint to the Toeplitz-Hilbert space construction. This 2-Categorical adjunction maintains the information both for the algebraic structure and the collection of positive linear functionals. Additionally, it accommodates variations of the Toeplitz-Hilbert space construction, defined by replacing the symmetric monoidal category of Hilbert spaces by an equivalent category obtained through a functor that preserves algebraic structure. A related 2-Categorical left adjoint, the Statues construction, is also discussed; it generates a C*-algebra from a given set of positive linear functionals, characterized by its ability to recognize equivalent categories of Hilbert spaces. The C*-algebra obtained through the Statues construction is topologically invariant, implying that the 2-Categorical left adjoint allows extension from the level of abstract C*-algebras to topological algebras. The 2-Categorical left adjoint also enables the recovery of the original C*-algebra from a given set of positive linear functionals, obtained through the combination of the GNS construction and the Toeplitz-Hilbert space construction, resulting in an isomorphic algebra to the original one. The process of obtaining this 2-Categorical left adjoint involves applying the monad obtained from the Toeplitz-Hilbert space construction, specifically its Eilenberg-Moore category, thereby generating a closure operator defined by application, or an operator that closes the given set of positive linear functionals under the relation of mutual inclusion. The resulting 2-Categorical left adjoint allows the recovery of the original C*-algebra from a given set of positive linear functionals by implementing a closure operator that identifies the algebraic structure as the minimal closed relation containing the given set of positive linear functionals. Recent discoveries of massive disks in radio galaxies not featuring active galactic nuclei not producing gamma-rays above 25 TeV not explain the massive deaths of stars.  The massive disks in these galaxies are likely captivated by magnetic fields and can function as powerful particle accelerators.  If this theory is correct, it would mean that everywhere in the universe there are massive disks generating gamma-rays from 10 MeV to 1 PeV.  This phenomenon would be caused by electron-positron pair production and gamma-ray absorption within the disks.  If this model for the disks is accurate, it would allow for a determination of the total baryon mass in the galaxies.  Furthermore, it would demonstrate the effectiveness of magnetic fields in the universe in this time period.  This discovery could also clarify the sources of high-energy neutrinos detected by the CHET and the TA, as well the massive deaths of stars, and star formation rates in the galaxies.  This theory can be tested using a gamma-ray telescope with a wide field of view, and a better understanding of the magnetic disks is crucial for achieving this goal.  This achievement would contribute significantly to the understanding of the universe, and could be accomplished within the time frame of an ongoing experiment, with a facility already in operation. Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by background noise and varying recording techniques.  To address this challenge, this study proposes a novel method for heart sound categorization that incorporates two key features to enhance accuracy: (1) combination of features derived from long short-term memory networks, and (2) inclusion of convolutional neural network-based features with additional noise and deformation models.  Experimental results show that the proposed method's performance in classifying normal and stenotic heart sounds in the PhysioNet Heart Sound Classification Dataset significantly outperforms existing approaches.  Specifically, this study's findings yield a significant improvement in accuracy (82.3%) when compared to the state-of-the-art techniques, which are comprised of a long short-term memory network, convolutional neural network, and an ensemble method.  Furthermore, the proposed approach's effectiveness in mitigating the adverse effects of background noise and recording deformation is substantiated in additional experiments.  The proposed method's superiority extends to accurately classifying sound recordings obtained from different sensors, which is a critical aspect in clinical settings.  The resulting model's compactness, in the form of a 2-class classifier with only 52 features, is another significant advantage.  The proposed method's efficacy is demonstrated in this study, and its potential is considerable, with possible applications in clinical settings beyond heart sound analysis.  One such promising area is speech recognition, where this method could likely yield comparable performance improvements.  The proposed approach's limitations, which arose during the long short-term memory-based feature extraction stage, are also discussed.  These challenges, although resolved in this study, could potentially obstruct the development of successful models in other contexts. The proliferation of wearable devices for monitoring physical and mental health enables rich biometric data, which can be utilized for precision medicine. However, wearables are often employed outside of controlled laboratory environments, compromising the accuracy of existing machine learning models. This challenge is magnified in a federated learning setting, where multiple individuals contribute their data towards a common goal while maintaining their privacy. To address this issue, an innovative transfer learning framework, FedHealth, is proposed to adapt models efficiently. FedHealth leverages two separate phases to improve accuracy: a transfer learning phase using federated learning to train models on combined data and a adaptation phase to fine-tune models on individual data. The proposed approach is demonstrated using biometric data from the Federal University of Pará, the University of Beira Interior, the University of Primeiro de Agosto, and the Technological Institute of Aeronautical Engineering, which are all widely available datasets. The results show that FedHealth outperforms conventional machine learning models in various scenarios. The proposed framework has numerous potential applications in wearable medical care. This study examines and contrasts various methods for managing portfolio risk, focusing on strategies that go beyond traditional mean-variance optimization. We review and analyze seven advanced methods, including three based on entropy, one using copulas, one utilizing a trust region, one with multiple objectives, and one using distributionally robust methods. We then apply and compare these methods to real-world data, covering both daily returns of 50 Nasdaq stocks and five individual asset returns. Our results show that the majority of these elevated methods outperform the basic mean-variance strategy in terms of portfolio performance. We also find that the methods using entropy and the distributionally robust method are more effective in achieving better results, with the entropy-based approaches generally yielding superior outcomes. We end by discussing the numerical costs of these methods to prepare for their potential use by institutional investors. The data used in this study is accessible via the Harvard Dataverse platform. The R code for the analysis is available upon request. The study also contributes a technical appendix discussing the details of the methods used. Finally, we will discuss the future of automated software and potential applications in areas like natural language processing, computer security, and statistical analysis. HDR photography combines multiple photos captured at various exposure levels to counterbalance overexposed and underexposed areas in a single image.  This technique minimizes the necessity to retake pictures and attenuates image post-processing workload.  Unfortunately, HDR creation remains a challenge, especially for amateur photographers, due to the complicated process of capturing and combining optimal images.  To address this issue, this study proposes an innovative, fully automated HDR-producing system specifically designed for camera-equipped mobile devices.  Once attached to the device's API, the HDR algorithm automatically determines the ideal exposure levels and captures three corresponding images.  These images are then undergo contrast-stretching and HDR fusion to produce a optimized HDR image.  To demonstrate the effectiveness of this proposed system, experimental evaluations were conducted on mobile devices including the Samsung Galaxy S4, Samsung Galaxy Note 3, and the iPhone 5s.  The findings show that our system generates HDR images of higher quality in terms of global contrast, color correction, and visual perception compared to the existing methods.  The open-source code for this research is available online.  In practice, this technology can be applied directly, without the need for complex post-processing, to produce HDR images on mobile devices equipped with high dynamic range capabilities.  In addition, this system serves as a platform for further research, such as advanced HDR capture, low-light level capture, and mobile image compression, among other possibilities.  The proposed algorithm's simplicity allows for easy integration into various mobile applications, including but not limited to live HDR video recording on smartphones, real-time HDR streaming, and various photography-related mobile games.  The detection method presented here can also be used independently to determine the optimal exposure level for standard photography. Causal neural networks, a emerging field in the realm of causal machine learning, aim to create resilient and trustworthy AI models by incorporating causal concepts into neural networks. This view acknowledges that learned representations in neural networks hold inherent value in their own right and can be valuable beyond simply using the generated class probabilities. This view is contested by some who see learned representations as simply a means to an end, with the primary purpose of classification. From this opposing perspective, alternative methods that focus on classification without considering the representation learning process can be more efficient. Both sides of this debate present interesting analysis techniques that can be used to interpret and understand learned representations and neural networks. This article is an invitation to collaborators to explore this topic with us, presenting methods to study the representation learning process in neural networks, and highlighting prominent research that treats learned representations as an end in themselves. We hope to further the discussion on the purpose and value of representation learning in neural networks. We also introduce the problem of navigating causal neural networks, the task of selecting the subset of features that directly support the predicted class, using the already trained neural network. This problem is significant because it can be used to remove redundant features, decrease overfitting, and even influence the robustness of the network. However, it also presents a hard challenge, given that neural networks are typically considered as black boxes. We outline our approach to solving this issue, introducing a novel algorithm called Causal Relevance Selection, that is effective in identifying the causal features for each data point. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach on real datasets, showing the positive impact it has on the performance, overfitting, and sparsity of the network. We also discuss the limitations of this approach and propose potential future work to further develop the field of causal neural networks. We believe this field has immense potential to contribute to the improvement of machine learning models and models based on deep learning. We hope this paper will pique the interest of researchers in this field and provide a starting point for further collaboration. We also make our code available to the public. The developed theory applies to both waveguides and optical resonators, considering their closed forms, and accounts for both linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions between the patterns. A recent study proposes a new approach for generating highly detailed images of turbulent flows at various Reynolds numbers using the principle of super-resolution restoration. This technique, achieved through the application of generative adversarial networks, involves creating a high-resolution image from a combination of lower-resolution images taken at the same position on an image array. A key innovation of this method is the development of a new algorithm that uses the spatial characteristics of noise in image arrays to determine optimal upscaling locations. This algorithm is distinct from traditional approaches that rely on the analysis of image frequency spectra. The proposed network successfully produces highly realistic high-resolution images when trained on a range of low-resolution images, and is effectively utilized to create highly detailed images of turbulent flows at various Reynolds numbers based on PIV data. This includes the generation of high-resolution velocity gradient images near the surface of a turbulent wave, as well as the generation of high-resolution streamfunction images in turbulent flows with periodic oscillations, and in flows with transient turbulent waves. The study demonstrates that the accuracy of these generated images can be further enhanced by comparing the computed velocity gradients with the actual PIV data, resulting in a network that provides unique insights into the spatial and temporal characteristics of turbulent flows. The proposed algorithm and network also show potential applications in the analysis of experimental data in turbulence research. The study includes an examination of the computational efficiency of the network, as well as the impact of noise on the effectiveness of the super-resolution restoration. The proposed framework is then utilized to investigate the dynamics of turbulent waves including the identification of coherent structures, the analysis of temporal oscillations, and the estimation of surface shear stress. The findings of the study are presented in a visual format through animated images of turbulent flows. The study provides a novel perspective on the analysis of experimental data in turbulence research, and highlights the importance of upscaling resolution in noise reduction in image arrays. The study also examines the relationship between the characteristic lengths of noise in image arrays and the characteristic lengths of turbulent flows, and presents a framework for its analysis. The study includes a discussion on the methods of upscaling resolution in image arrays and the associated challenges, as well as the advantages of super-resolution restoration in turbulence research, including the detection of outliers in noise, the enhancement of image quality near edges and surfaces, and the improvement of coherence in coherent structures. This note provides an introduction to the interplay between algebraic and geometric concepts in developing compactifications for moduli spaces. We examine the relationship between certain algebraic compactifications and geometric compactifications using boundary actions of discrete groups. Specifically, we investigate the connection between certain algebraic compactifications and geometric compactifications via boundary actions of discrete groups. However, this relationship is not universal and we discuss instances where it fails. Moreover, we outline an approach using geometric compactifications and boundary actions of discrete groups to construct compactifications for moduli spaces, along with an associated compactification type known as an Borel-Siudeckis compactification. Furthermore, we discuss the connection between Neron models and Borel-Siudeckis compactifications. Additionally, we provide a brief overview of various specific examples, including spaces of elliptic curves, genus two curves, and curves of higher genus. The note concludes by examining the connection between the geometric compactification type known as an Neron model and the algebraic compactification type known as an Min\'o-Yu compactification. Determining the factors that control the shape of the mass-starformation rate function, particularly its turn-over at high masses, is crucial for accurate measurements of the total gas reservoir of galaxies. Using a comprehensive, publicly available database of spectroscopically identified galaxies, we investigated the mass-star formation rate (M-SFR) and bulge-to-total ratio (B/T) collections to analyze the mass-star formation rate function and explore its dependence on bulge growth. Our results show that an increase in B/T values corresponds to a decrease in SFRs for all galaxy masses. Furthermore, we found that the distinction between bulge-forming and star-forming galaxies is marked, with the former exhibiting higher masses and lower SFRs. Our data also indicate that the characteristic star formation rates of galaxies with different masses show a weaker correlation compared to previous studies, suggesting that the mass-Star Formation Rate (SFR) relation becomes flatter at higher masses. We propose a new model that describes the connection between bulge growth and the transformation of gas into stars, and uses this model to explain the observed turn-over of the M-SFR relation, with masses greater than ~10 to the 10.5 solar masses. This value is supported by numerous observational studies that have established the typical masses of bulge-forming galaxies and the contribution of active galactic nuclei to the SFRs of galaxies with the highest masses. Our analysis suggests that the diversity of SFRs within a particular mass range provides valuable information about the physical processes that govern galaxy evolution, and that a single mass-SFR relation cannot describe the behavior of all galaxies, citing examples of disk-dominated galaxies with high SFRs and massive bulge-dominated galaxies with low SFRs. Our research also yields a specific prediction regarding the shape of the mass-SFR function for galaxies with massive bulge components and active galactic nuclei, with predictions that can be tested by future observations. Finally, our findings emphasize the importance of distinguishing between different types of galaxies when analyzing their mass distributions and the role of bulge growth in star formation rates. Our research has implications for various theoretical models of galaxy evolution and provides a new perspective on the mass-SFR relation, with potential applications to a wide range of observational and theoretical contexts. Our analysis has been extended to investigate the relationship between the stellar mass of galaxies and their gas reservoirs, with results that reflect the influence of bulge growth and offer a distinct insight into the mechanisms that govern galaxy evolution. Due to the burgeoning need for emotional support, cross-lingual sentiment analysis on social media has become increasingly vital. This task involves categorizing posts written in languages other than the analyst's native tongue in terms of their emotional content, a skill that can be helpful not only to language learners but also to speakers of the same language who need assistance with multiple languages. In cross-lingual sentiment analysis, researchers often rely on trained multilingual models, which can be applied to various languages. However, utilizing these models comes at a cost, given their substantial size. To address the challenge of small-sample-size, we introduce a flexible, multi-task learning-based framework called $\ell$-MTTL, which is capable of handling both large-scale pre-trained models as tasks. This framework's ability to determine the ideal number of tasks automatically makes it suitable for cross-lingual applications. Evaluations using multiple languages have shown that our method outperforms the current state-of-the-art in low-resource settings and matches the performance of state-of-the-art methods in medium-resource settings. Moreover, our analysis reveals that the ideal number of tasks influences the model's performance, with the optimal number dependent on the amount of data available. In addition, we discovered that the model's performance improves when it is trained on similar tasks that differ only in their language when there is a large amount of data available. Our code is available at GitHub: https://github.com/lingua-terra/mttl.

The simplicial bundle construction, initially introduced by Bousfield and Kan, has been a significant tool in simplicial homotopy theory. We show that the global simplicial bundle construction over a paracompact space can be interpreted as a simplicial group action, building on the work of Bousfield and Kan. This action is determined by the simplicial set acting on the simplicial space and the simplicial map between them. This perspective provides a simpler proof of a result stated by Bousfield and Kan and also enables us to establish an analogous result for simplicial algebras over a monad. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the global simplicial bundle is invariant under reymannian retractions and show that it inherits simplicial properties such as being a simplicial group or a simplicial category. We also introduce a variant of the global simplicial bundle that is applicable to simplicial objects in a base category $\mathcal{C}$, showing that it yields a simplicial object in the base category $\mathcal{C}$. This variant is found to be useful in specifically geometric applications. The work presented here also draws connections to the work of Grandis and Lucaroni on bundle constructions in the context of abstract structures. A recent observation of a massive hot dense spin of a solar-type star, likely the result of a planetary disruption, has sparked interest in understanding the potential for planets to exist in the star's inner zone. To combat the instability of planetary orbits in this region, researchers propose that stars' angular momentum must be disrupted by planets there. In the case of solar-like stars, this would make their outer layers spin more rapidly. However, by modeling angular momentum generated by planets in the inner zone, we find that its effect on the stars' outer spin and mass loss is minimal. Consequently, a small fleet of planets in the inner zone is not sufficient to explain the observed rapid spin of the star in question. Furthermore, such a planetary system would actually result in the star's surface spinning more slowly, due to tidal interactions causing the spin to slow. Therefore, alternative mechanisms are likely responsible for this particular observed phenomenon. In the broader context, we find that the migration phase of planets primarily serves to increase a star's rotational slowdown, rather than slowing it down. This could have implications for exoplanet detection, as dense stars with a high surface gravity are more likely to have detected planets than those with low surface gravity. On the other long-lived, massive stars with low surface gravity are less likely to have detected planets than those with a higher surface gravity. Finally, by comparing various detection methods, we find that the most effective exoplanet detection technique for solar-type stars would be the Transit Method, particularly the Eagle-Nebula Protocol. Alternatively, one-star eclipse searches could also be viable. Fake news poses a significant information threat on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and potential to cause harm globally. To address this issue, technologies for detecting false news are urgently needed. The sheer variety of false news articles makes it impractical to develop tailored detection systems for every individual case, making it essential to create more flexible emergence-based methods that can adapt to new false news instances. In this paper, a method is presented that utilizes interaction history to enhance its ability to identify new false news, and the interaction history is defined as a combination of media content and user feedback. The proposed framework, leveraging the Metanp framework, incorporates two levels of adaptation: the first level, where the system learns general false news characteristics; and the second level, where it learns from specific data. The effectiveness of the proposed network is demonstrated in multiple experiments, where it outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in Facebook's DeepFake detection data set and the Multimodal Emergent False News Identification Data Set. The findings have been published in two separate papers, namely the false news detection paper and the education paper. The code is available for public use at https://github.com/ChengxiangCao/MetaNPFN.

A method for constructing a an NGCP is described using complementary triads and biplanes. Specifically, it is shown that a particular type of pair, called a "full NGCP", can be created when a large set with a specific property exists – this property is referred to as the "extended Golay property". A set of size $8$ with the extended Golay property serves as the fundamental building block, enabling the generation of larger sets with the same property. A few examples of constructions for various set sizes are provided, in addition to a full NGCP and a pair of complementary sets from a specific type of large sequence array. Moreover, this work paves the way for exploring extensions of the extended Golay property to larger sequence lengths. In addition, a brief discussion on the relationship between biplanes, complementary triads, and the extended Golay property is presented. In recent years, multi-channel speech processing has gained significant attention, and techniques such as differential microphones have been widely used in various applications. However, speech recorded using this method suffers from interference and requires sophisticated restoration techniques for effective noise reduction tools like speech recognition systems. Previous studies primarily focused on two-channel speech restoration, whereas the possibility of expanding related techniques to individual-channel speech improvement has been underexploited. This paper introduces a new model, the Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN), which efficiently employs two-channel information to enhance a single channel. Unlike existing approaches that rely on deep learning models combining inter-channel and intra-channel information, DPCRN leverages convolutional recurrent networks to exploit patterns within each channel and convolutive connections between channels. A nonlinear interaction occurs between electromagnetic fields in quantum electrodynamics, resulting in vacuum polarization. This interaction can lead to a new field of non-linear electrodynamics that affects black hole physics, specifically when it pertains to the Einstein-power-Yang-Mills (EPYM) gravity framework. We examine the connection between an observable, shadow radius, and a first-order phase transition in a nonlinear, charged AdS black hole within the EPYM gravity context. Analyzing this relationship, we identify conditions that allow for non-monotonic behavior among shadow radius, horizon radius, and temperature. Moreover, we observe that the phase transition temperature can differ based on whether we consider the shadow radius or the horizon radius. These findings suggest that the shadow radius is an effective probe for revealing phase transition information in black holes. We further analyze the thermal profiles of big and small black hole coexistence phases under distinct non-linear YM charge parameter values ($\gamma = 1$ and $\gamma = 1.5$), in addition to the impact of this parameter on shadow radius and thermal profile behavior. Our analysis indicates that both black hole heat capacity and shadow radius exhibit step-like behavior during phase transitions. We also find that the shadow radius can serve as a probe for thermal profile variations in black holes. Consequently, the radial extent of a black hole shadow can be influenced by a first-order phase transition, even when the change in the black hole's electric charge is topologically discrete. This effect allows us to recover the underlying physics through observations of the M87* black hole, specifically its shadow radius and thermal environment. Tensor network methods have historically been utilized in the representation of physical states, allowing for the implementation of efficient numerical techniques for various systems, especially those featuring strong interactions across a 1D chain of spins. However, the application of these methods to describe thermal equilibrium and dynamic scenarios has been hinderly challenging due to the inherent incompatibility of positive semi-definite matrices in the tensor construction. A novel framework, the "locally precise tensor network method," has been developed to overcome this limitation. This approach combines the benefits of precise representation and efficient computation, offering a powerful tool for exploring complex many-body systems. The efficacy of this method is illustrated in a comparison with the widely used multi-scale tensor network approach, demonstrating its superiority for low-temperature scenarios. We introduce the concept of a hypernymic approximation, which allows for the decoupling of complex hypernyms into separate approximations of their hyponyms. This strategy enables the evaluation of individual aspects of a complex concept without being influenced by other, potentially conflicting facets. We demonstrate the utility of this approach in a number of contexts, including the integration of conflicting rules in reasoning, the interpretation of ambiguous words with multiple related meanings, and the computation of similarity between concepts. Furthermore, we show that any question that can be answered about a hypernym also can be answered about its approximation, providing a decoupling of attributes that otherwise might be in conflict. However, we note that the accuracy of these approximations is necessary for the validity of these results. The proposed hypernymic approximation framework is applicable to a broad range of representation formats, including description logics, semantic networks, and frames. The source code for the proposed method has been made publicly available on GitHub. The resulting scale-oriented approximation is a multi-faceted evaluation that accounts for various aspects of a complex concept, including its relationships with other concepts, its level of efficacy, the sources that subscribe to it, and the degree of this subscription. The scale-oriented approximation facilitates the identification of the specific aspect of a complex concept that is being evaluated, as well as the recognition of the method of this evaluation. A patterned metal film, part of a lattice, sits on a reflective surface and is covered by a thin layer that can be oriented in three dimensions. When light hits the pattern, it interacts with the embedded layer based on its orientation and can result in counter-intuitive effects known as Rayleigh-Benard convection patterns due to temperature gradients caused by light absorption. Despite this challenge, it has been demonstrated that a shallow neural network can determine if a dataset is suitable for a deep network to use. In this paper, a novel framework is introduced that leverages a black-box model to determine suitable datasets and levers the principle of opposite learning to transfer knowledge from a model that has access to the target dataset. This new framework can be used for tasks such as selecting the most effective dataset for training and evaluating fake data generation. By using a model that has never seen the data, the quality of selected samples can be assessed, without being contaminated by the model's own generation errors. This paper's contributions are reflected in its performance in various tasks, as shown in the experimental results presented. Researchers have observed the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_L$ decay mode for the first time, and have also gathered evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_L$ decay mode, utilizing a 3.0 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ dataset of $pp$ collisions collected at 7 and 8 TeV center-of-mass energies by the LHCb. The branching fractions for these decays are calculated as follows: The $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 \bar{K}^0$ branching fraction is estimated at (4.3±0.5±0.3±0.3±0.6) ×10^-4, and the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} \bar{K}^0$ branching fraction is estimated at (2.8±1.0±0.3±0.2±0.4) ×10^-4, with the given uncertainties stemming from various sources. These decays primarily proceed through the electroweak penguin diagram, providing valuable insights into the study of the CKM unitary triangle and the charm quark sector. Additionally, the measurement of the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_L$ decay rate allows for the determination of the $B^0_s$ meson decay constant, resulting in $|f_{B_s}|$ at 3.0 GeV, with an uncertainty of 4%. Furthermore, the analysis of these decays involves counting the number of neutral kaon charges, which may have implications for the understanding of the $B^0_s\to\gamma\gamma$ decay rate and the $B^0_s$ oscillation amplitude. The study of these decays at future facilities, such as the LHCb upgrade and the Super KeK, has the potential to significantly reduce the uncertainties associated with these measurements. The rising popularity of autonomous systems faces challenges due to the need for extensive training and potential safety constraints when learning from multiple agents simultaneously. A new setting, co-observation learning, is introduced to address these difficulties by enabling agents to learn from each other's experiences without an expert display of actions. In this setting, agents take turns observing and acting, and the learner aims to match the performance of the active agent based on the observed actions and rewards. A framework is provided to guide future research in this newly explored area of co-observation learning. The framework considers various scenarios, including those with shared or distinct action and reward observations, as well as different observation ranges. Existing solutions can learn from current methods such as inverse reinforcement learning and can be applied to problematic situations like multi-agent collision avoidance. The chapter also delves into specific cases like a simple Markov decision process and a deep reinforcement learning-based system. Finally, potential approaches and challenges in co-observation learning without an expert display of actions are discussed. The chapter concludes by examining the relationship between co-observation learning and other researched topics in reinforcement learning. The chapter is organized as follows. The background and problem definition are presented in Section I. The framework of co-observation learning is introduced in Section II. The general approach to co-observation learning without an expert display of actions is discussed in Section III. The special case of action-observation reinforcement learning is examined in Section IV. The chapter concludes in Section V. The appendix is presented in Section VI. MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented NoSQL database that has gained
significant popularity in recent years. Despite its success, MongoDB's
transactional functionality remains poorly understood. Unlike relational
databases, MongoDB's transactions are coupled with its optimistic concurrency
control, making it essential to validate concurrency conditions within which
transactions are successful. However, available research focuses primarily on
validating data integrity in update operations, neglecting concurrency control.
Concurrently, the MongoDB community is awaiting enhancements to its concurrency
control, hoping it will lead to better performance and throughput.

Although these problems have been well-known for many decades, their solutions remained elusive until the present day. This article will demonstrate that utilizing the framework of distance functions between subspaces, the original questions intended by Menger can be answered. Specifically, we can determine when the sum of distances between pairs of points from different spaces is equivalent to the distance between points from the same space, as well as identify the spaces in which the angle between subspaces is hereditary. Additionally, we show that these scenarios are characterized by specific properties of the original metric space. Furthermore, our results can be applied to determine the conditions under which the Lasserre relaxation of a given integer program yields an integer solution, as this is equivalent to the original space containing the information about the angles between its subspaces, thereby hereditarily capturing this information. Our article also includes a discussion of this idea in the specific setting of polynomial moments. Moreover, we provide a framework for extending our results to more general contexts, as well as a vast number of specific examples and counterexamples that demonstrate the versatility and relevance of our results. Despite the solutions to Menger's problems being known for many decades, they have been known under different names in the mathematical community. Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been unfeasible until now. This research undertakes an empirical analysis of Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scheme built into a blockchain smart contract, with a public transaction record that allows us to map its structure using network analysis tools. By utilizing Ethereum block chain data and a custom-made dataset compilation method, our study presents an overview of the scheme's evolution, a statistical breakdown of its components, and a detailed examination of participant hierarchies, as well as a review of the problems faced by its operators. By analyzing hidden transactions, we are able to reconstruct Forsage's structure, revealing the scam's extensive extent and revealing patterns of activity among its participants. Our findings were previously unknown to the public and have been shared with the relevant authorities. Our research highlights the difficulties in detecting and combating pyramid schemes, as well as the need for greater transparency in the cryptocurrency industry. Moreover, our analysis facilitates a deeper understanding of the precarious stability of pyramid schemes, showcasing how changes in withdrawal rules can influence their operation and eventual collapse. Our work with Forsage serves as a case study, with implications that can be applied to other blockchain-based pyramid schemes. Ultimately, our goal in conducting this investigation was to aid in the capture of its operators, as well as to contribute to the development of effective methods for detecting and preventing pyramid schemes built into smart contracts. Our research with Forsage also provides a framework for examining the truthfulness of smart contract owners, with consequences for the integrity of blockchain-based applications similar to Forsage. Our analysis of Forsage's structure was made possible by the transparency of its transactions, a feature that is uncommon in typical blockchain transactions, with implications for how easily similar schemes could be hidden in the future, as well as for the difficulty of identifying recent participants in similar schemes. The catalog of the Milky Way bulge's globular clusters compiled by Ornitelli et al. (2020) was investigated using data from the VVV survey. The study analyzed the catalog's entries for the 19 proposed clusters with limited information and conducted a detailed investigation to confirm their status as globular clusters. The research involved creating a catalog of likely cluster members based on positional coordinates, determining concentration profiles for the clusters, calculating key astrophysical properties including horizontal branch magnitudes, and comparing the clusters to various definitions of the bulge population. The findings suggest that 14 of the 19 clusters likely reside in the bulge and are part of the galaxy's globular cluster population. However, only three have complete Hertzsprung-Russell diagrams similar to those of established bulge globular clusters. The study also discovered several clusters that may be foreground or background clusters. The condition of several clusters is questionable due to limited data, and more comprehensive investigations are necessary to confirm their classification as globular clusters. The study utilized a conservative approach to define the galactic bulge's globular cluster population based on metallicity and horizontal branch type, finding that the bulge's globular clusters fall within a specific range of these parameters. The research included a discussion of the clusters' possible variable star populations and suggested stellar masses based on mass-function analyses. The study concluded by highlighting the need for additional observational data, particularly in the form of multi-color photometry and spectroscopy, to confirm the catalog entries and further investigate the galaxy's bulge cluster population. The associated catalog of cluster and stellar properties is available electronically. Deep learning techniques have recently been successfully applied in various contexts beyond the traditional operational management models and theories. This study explores the current state of deep learning applications relating to business forecasting. We conduct a comparative analysis of 12 Schumpeterian innovation waves involving prophesied, analyzed, and anticipated values for 4 significant business indicators: GDP, unemployment rates, stock prices, and company profits. Our primary research employs a combination of LSTM, GRU, and vanilla RNN networks to predict the indicators based on historical data and evaluates different deep learning approaches to determine their effectiveness. Our study reveals that, regardless of indicator or innovation wave, the best predictions are obtained using LSTM networks. We also find that the R2 score and MAE for all indicators surpass the baseline values established through simple exponential smoothing methods. Additionally, our research highlights the importance of considering the size of the training data to achieve optimal results and emphasizes the necessity of further validation to ensure the generalizability of our findings. The massive, grid-like near-ultraviolet structure observed in the 1985 eruption of the classical nova AD Leo is reported, based on newly discovered images from the SkyMap project. This phenomenon is now known to occur in several other novae and supernovae, characterized by a pattern of rays that emanate from a developing jet. A previously proposed model, which includes both high-velocity jets and shedding of hot and dense matter, successfully explains the spatial distribution and spectral properties of the 1985 eruption of AD Leo. However, this study goes further in comparing its own observations with the model, by analyzing the spectral lines' strengths and shapes, and finding that the rays and the remaining material have similar chemical compositions. Furthermore, it is discovered that the hottest rays initially dominated the spectrum, before the cooler rays took over, and that the model's prediction of a decreasing temperature over time is consistent with the observed data. The model's success in explaining the structure and evolution of the 1985 eruption of AD Leo, using both its spatial and spectral characteristics, is demonstrated in this study. The novelty of this research is marked by the discovery of UV images from the SkyMap project, the most comprehensive set of near-ultraviolet spectra for a nova eruption to date, the observation of a decreasing temperature across the rays and the remaining material, and the unique perspective gained from this research, which highlights the importance of considering the shedding of matter and the effects of absorption and scattering when studying the earliest moments of transient astrophysical events. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) rely on two interconnected components: a generator creating fake data resembling the target distribution and a discriminator differentiating real data from fabricated information. In standard GAN training, both the generator and discriminator are equally developed through simultaneous training, which can result in the generator outperforming the discriminator by creating very realistic data, making it difficult for the discriminator to distinguish correctly. To address this issue, we propose the SparseGAN framework, which incorporates a novel sparse training design for both the generator and discriminator. By adopting a sparse training approach, we introduce dropout layers both for the generator and discriminator, and impose a non-decreasing sparsity schedule on them. As data passes through these dropout layers, it takes on noisy characteristics similar to sample outputs from the generator and misleading information from the discriminator. This configuration enables the generator and discriminator to learn from each other's mistakes and incorrect judgments in isolated processes, allowing them to develop distinct perspectives. We demonstrate the efficacy of SparseGAN through multiple experiments on generative models, revealing that it outperforms baseline GAN models in various assessment metrics. Furthermore, we find that SparseGAN's capabilities extend beyond GAN training, allowing it to be a versatile framework for enhancing existing models in various tasks, including classification and generation. To accommodate complex, large-scale datasets, we propose a scalable version of SparseGAN, along with sample code available online. This framework and our findings are applicable to various GAN-based text generation scenarios, including conversation starters, summarization, and classification. We also explore this scalable version's performance on massive datasets, including Wikipedia articles and Amazon product reviews, showing its potential for large-scale text creation and subsequent analysis. This research is distinct from standard GAN training and opens up new possibilities for both sparse learning and GAN-based text generation scenarios. The code for SparseGAN is available at https://github.com{:/user/abc123whisker/SparseGAN}.

The idea that life could be transferred from one planetary system to another through panspermia, potentially facilitated by interstellar travel, is both captivating and complex. While this concept is intriguing, it's also challenging to evaluate, given the limited data available. A key obstacle in assessing the validity of interstellar panspermia is determining the extent to the capability of detecting viable microorganisms on comet-like objects, particularly within the inner regions of a system that has hosted a close approach to a star similar to the Sun. In this work, a focus is placed on investigating the viability of detecting signs of interstellar panspermia through astronomical means by examining the survival rates of bacteria on comet Sentry-2009 (C/2009 K5), combined with astrophysical modeling of comet destruction and a statistical analysis of interstellar comet trajectories. A novel detection method for viable microorganisms is proposed, based on measuring the absorption of ultraviolet light by bacterial DNA. A preliminary assessment suggests that detecting this effect could be feasible with the help of upcoming telescopes equipped with high-resolution UV spectrographs. According to our calculations, the likelihood of discovering evidence of interstellar panspermia in the inner regions of a system that has hosted a close approach to a star similar to the Sun could be as low as 10^-4, given current capabilities and assuming a typical comet trajectory. However, this value is expected to drop significantly as future capabilities improve. In the optimal case, the viability of this detection method could be as high as 10^-3 with the help of the James Webb Space Telescope, given its superior sensitivity and the presence of suitable comet trajectories. In contrast, a negative result could provide vital insights into the low bounds of survival rates of bacteria on comets, with implications for the effectiveness of panspermia. Animal population studies and conservation efforts can greatly benefit from combining two essential methods: Spatial Capture-Recapture analysis and Resource Selection Functions. Capture-Recapture statistics provide essential information about the size and density of a population, while Resource Selection Functions indicate the species' preference for specific habitats. We examine the challenge of developing accurate representations of large networks from limited local views in networks that are prone to malicious node attacks. To achieve a precise global representation, we propose a decentralized estimation approach called VSGE, which adapts to changes in the network freely and produces estimates with statistically verifiable precision. Distinguishing VSGE from existing aggregation protocols, our algorithm ensures the accuracy of its estimates in small worlds, even when the percentage of malicious nodes exceeds the network's diameter. We also establish a key precision accuracy trade-off for  random networks without a small-world properties. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of VSGE in realistic networks by conducting a series of simulation experiments using real-world datasets. Our results show that VSGE outperforms existing approaches in various network configurations and robustness levels. We also explore the connection between the algorithm's precision and the network's component count, node degree, and geographic dispersion, uncovering insights that can guide the design of scalable and accurate network estimation systems. We complement our simulation studies with a real-world implementation of VSGE on the LOFAR telescope network, showing that the algorithm's precision can be maintained in dynamic networks with changing node degrees and component structures. We also discuss various design choices and possible further enhancements of VSGE. Lastly, we outline possible future directions for extending the algorithm to handle changing network topologies and complex dynamics. All the simulation code and datasets used in this research are available at https://github.com/ghulamai/NSE-Simulation.

These problems fall under the umbrella of a specific problem type where the relationship between the size of the object and the clearance is defined by a particular type of function called a weak-would-be-quadratic. Our main achievement is to demonstrate that for these problems, any solution with a certain level of symmetry, also exhibits a particular uniform level of symmetry. It also extends the previous results of Kristanovich and Levenshtein, by removing the need for a level of symmetry equivalent to the full object and instead allows for the level of symmetry to be only partially realized. Recent advancements in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have made significant progress in recovering mobility in patients with spinal cord injuries. Historically, these systems have focused on upper body function recovery but have given limited attention to restoring lower body mobility. A major limitation of existing BCIs for lower body recovery is the lack of accurate prediction of step frequency, a crucial aspect for smooth gait. In this study, we accurately predicted step frequencies in addition to identifying ambulatory states from electrocorticogram (ECoG) signals in a tetraplegic patient. Our findings showed that we could identify the patient's ambulatory state with over 90% accuracy and predict step frequencies with a mean absolute error of 10.6 steps per minute. These results demonstrate a significant advancement in BCIs for lower body recovery and provide a promising platform for future gait frequency prediction and state detection. Furthermore, this research highlights the potential of high-resolution gait models enabled by advanced BCIs, which could be crucial in treating spinal cord injuries. A key challenge remaining is to develop a system that can be used by patients with similar injuries. This study's findings contribute to the limited research on BCIs for lower body recovery, especially step frequency prediction, and provide a valuable insight into the relationship between brain activity and step frequency through a high-resolution gait model. This research also provides a novel perspective on the rehabilitation of spinal cord injuries, with a particular focus on gait recovery, by exploring the relationship between different ambulatory states, brain activity, and step frequencies, which could be invaluable for healthcare professionals, neuroscientists, and the patient community. This work's significance has been further emphasized by the award it received at the 2020 IEEE/RAS-EMBS International Conference on Intelligent Systems for Molecular Biology and Bioinformatics and the 2021 National Institute of Health's Highly Cited Paper Award. Our research involves examining the underlying assumptions of the event form encoding approach, which converts raw collision data into events for subsequent analysis, specifically for our study of the ALICE experiment at the CERN LHC. By exploring different event encoding assumptions, we investigated the impact of event selection on measured particle distributions, such as the transverse momentum ($p_T$) of pions, kaons, and protons in central Pb-Pb collisions at a collision energy of $\sqrt{s_\rm{NN}}=2.76$ TeV. Our analysis showed that the event encoding assumptions are crucial, particularly in the context of particle momentum measurements, as they influence the magnitude of elliptical flow patterns. To validate our findings, we compared our results with actual ALICE experiment data, utilizing events simulated with the HYDRO++ code. Our study identified areas where the event encoding approach breaks down and found that the encoding of flow patterns is encoded too simply, meaning that the approach fails to accurately capture the unique features of collision events. Therefore, any analysis relying on this approach, such as particle distribution measurements in heavy-ion collisions, may be compromised. Consequently, we recommend re-examining the event encoding method, possibly by incorporating additional features that capture the complex structure of collision events, especially elliptical flow patterns, to ensure the validity of research based on this approach. This article presents an innovative approach to achieving a better understanding of a specific Diophantine equation that has been extensively studied. Originally introduced by Alfred van der Poorten in 1980, the equation $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$ was a key component in his work on equations involving powers of prime numbers. Building upon his findings, we establish a significant result by demonstrating that all solutions to the equation can be formatted into a specific two-factorial structure, effectively capturing all possible combinations of the variables $a$ and $b$ for any given nonnegative integer $n$. Furthermore, we show that this approach leads to the conclusion that the equation has only a limited number of solutions, namely those where the absolute value of $a$ or $b$ equals $1$ or $7$ for any given $n$. Additionally, we derive a related result from this approach, the result being that the equation $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$ has only two solutions in the domain of positive integers, namely $(a,b)=(7,7)$ when $n=3$ and $(a,b)=(1,7)$ when $n=5$. The article also examines various equivalent forms of the equation and presents two such forms, forms that can be derived from the basic form $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$ through the application of algebraic manipulations. The article further delves into the concept of its solutions in the domain of whole numbers by introducing the term '7-number'. A 7-number is defined as a whole number that can be expressed in the form $a^2+ab+b^2$ for some given $a$ and $b$. Our study examines the impact of screening from adjacent electrons on the onset of charge or magnetic ordering due to Coulomb interaction in a dual-band model for infinite-layer nickelate. Furthermore, a longer-range Coulomb interaction indicates that the system prefers to be at a filling that is further removed from half-filling, which may explain the observed absence of charge or magnetic ordering in infinite-layer nickelate. This result extends the renowned Liouville theorem and provides a novel proof of its extended form. To effectively address open-domain commonsense question answering, it's essential to explore methods that analyze the connection between questions and available web documents. Current approaches primarily focus on incorporating rich representations, without sufficient attention to the semantic connections between questions and documents. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel approach, called Coarse-to-Precise, which first employs a question-document pair rejection model to eliminate non-relevant documents, resulting in a smaller, more precise set of documents. This approach facilitates the creation of more intricate representations, with a focus on capturing the semantic relationships between questions and the remaining documents. We further enhance the representation by incorporating a question-document attention mechanism and a semantic-aware mask model. The Coarse-to-Precise approach outperforms the current state-of-the-art models on the CommonsenseQA and ReCo datasets, with notable improvements of 1.05% and 2.13% in the exact match score, and 0.74% and 1.53% in the F1 score, respectively. The code is available at https://github.com/ghru/Coarse-to-Precise.

This paper introduces the Random Stroll Method (RSM) to address challenges in Federated Learning (FL) across diverse data. Institutions with different privacy regulations and various dataset characteristics participate in FL. This diversity hinders data sharing and collaborative learning. RSM addresses this issue by applying a stochastic exploration technique within the institutions. Each participant explores their local data by generating diverse instances, which enhances the representation and improves performance. RSM also incorporates an adaptive strategy to strike a balance between model update and data exploration, thereby preventing the model from drifting too far from its initial state. The results show that RSM outperforms the baseline in various settings and is more efficient than incremental learning. RSM demonstrates comparable performance to vanilla FL in a numerical experiment and exhibits benefits in models with rich features. Furthermore, RSM shows potential in combining datasets with different dataset characteristics. The source code for RSM is available online. This research was funded by the National Natural Science Foundation of China and the Guangdong Provincial Key Laboratory of Big Data Intelligence Engineering. A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper addresses that challenge by introducing a new technique to enhance semi-supervised image segmentation. The proposed method involves training a network with two outputs: one for segmentation and one for classification, using only the existing partial annotations to define a regularizer. The network is trained to ensure the segmentation and classification results align for pixels marked as certain, which provides a regularizer to guide the segmentation task. The proposed technique is versatile, and we show that using a pre-trained model as the classification network yields superior results, which we call the Proposed Versatile Model, resulting in a 3.5% Dice score on average and 21.4% on the minimum Dice score in both experiments. Recently, convincing performance has been achieved by Mandarin Speech Recognition using public models trained on English data. However, the underlying factors behind this success are not well understood. In this work, we investigate the source of these results and explore methods to break cultural barriers in ASR. We discover that the primary source of this success is due to the high quality of Mandarin training data, specifically because of the prevalence of Chinese characters in the names, although this character name structure is not widespread. To further expand the scope of our findings, we design a novel experiment using a small amount of data with a similar character name structure in a different language, Japanese. Our results show that Mandarin ASR models can be easily trained to handle Japanese names with a similar structure, without experiencing an increase in error rate. Moreover, we discover a significant decrease in error rates when transferring models from a smaller language group, specifically between Japanese and Mandarin, likely due to the similarity in character sets. Our research is the first to successfully implement cross-language and cross-script ASR transfer using simple data techniques. We believe that our findings have the potential to challenge current ideas about the success of zero-shot ASR, and demonstrate that character-based models may benefit from a more nuanced understanding, given the prevalence of characters in names. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghru/rough-to-fine-asr.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 10 actions per second, largely because of the rigorous rule-based checking process for action validity.
This slow pace makes it difficult to conduct multiple million-step trials, a common benchmark in evaluating large-language model performance.
In response to these constraints, we present TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three popular text-based games, specifically designed to handle high-speed evaluations. Unlike the original versions, TextWorldExpress games employ a data-driven approach to assess action validity, resulting in a significant boost in processing speed to over one million steps per second on a single GPU. When put to the test, this accelerated version allows for the completion of multiple million-step trials with various large-language models, yielding precise and reliable performance metrics. The enhanced framework and reference benchmarks are available to the public, paving the way for future large-scale evaluations of text-based games. With the current record of over 1.5 million steps per second on a single A100 GPU, there's ample room for further optimization, offering opportunities for researchers to contribute to the community by improving the performance of TextWorldExpress. The underlying framework of TextWorldExpress is versatile and applicable to any text-based game that can be framed around a central state table, offering a broad range of possibilities for further innovation, including multi-player games and more complex evaluation protocols. The benchmark data for TextWorldExpress is extensive, comprising over 200 million words across three games, making it an valuable resource for developers and researchers alike. The framework and reference benchmarks for TextWorldExpress are available at https://textworldexpress.org/.

In this article, a characterization of the ring's property of being F-local is provided, with the characterization involving the tight Hilbert polynomials of its local components. Additionally, we offer a method for determining the ring's F-rank, achieving this rank as the smallest degree of all local components' tight Hilbert polynomials. Furthermore, a lower bound on the ring's depth is established, with this lower bound equal to the smallest degree of all local components' tight Hilbert polynomials minus one. A special case study involving a specific local ring is also presented. To improve the effectiveness of sentence ranking systems for machine comprehension, research aims to explicitly train these models using discourse indicators. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have gained widespread acceptance for various image classification tasks. Despite their success, CNNs are prone to performance degradation under certain environmental conditions, such as temperature fluctuations and aging effects, which cause faults in hardware. To address this issue, research has focused on validating that CNNs are resilient to these faults. In this work, we investigate the resistance of CNNs to hardware faults by analyzing how they handle interval variations in activation values. We propose a method that determines the interval in which activation values should fall, thus ensuring the correctness of output classifications. To validate this approach, we tested it using a CNN on two image classification datasets, with the results showing that a robust interval can be identified to ensure accurate classifications for new, unseen data. In particular, our approach yielded a success rate of 98.08% for the CIFAR-10 dataset and 94.57% for the MNIST dataset. These findings provide a security guarantee for CNNs against faults caused by finite precision hardware, as well as physical environments affected by temperature fluctuations. Multilingual modeling has been highly successful in translating between multiple languages, but managing the diverse structures of different languages remains a challenge. We analyze the approach of multilingual BERT, a type of neural network used for language analysis, and uncover the underlying representation of its language criteria. Our investigation reveals that multilingual BERT operates under a single shared multilingual vector space that combines the semantic content of different languages. However, this space retains distinct substructures for each language, allowing it to capture their unique characteristics. We further develop a method to extract these substructures into separate vector spaces, one for each language, while preserving the shared multilingual vector space. Our approach and representation, which we call CWS, have several benefits, including enabling smooth transitions between languages, reducing cognitive discomfort, and facilitating cross-language understanding. Our evaluation, conducted using multilingual BERT, shows that CWS successfully captures the intrinsic characteristics of each language and yields notable improvements in cross-language tasks, including translation and grammar checking. When applied to real datasets, CWS achieves superior performance, with results showing that it outperforms the current state-of-the-art methods by 1.5% in accuracy and 5.8% in F1-score. Our code is available online at https://github.com/ghrua/Multi-lingual-Shared-Semantic-Space.

To tackle this problem, we design a deep neural network named EMA-VIO by drawing on the concept of external memory, and it integrates information from various sources including imaging, inertial, and previous estimates to make predictions. This paper proposes a new framework called Federated Selective Integration (FSI) to address the challenges of varying data quality and insufficient data, particularly in the context of sensitive and large-scale healthcare information. Within the FSI framework, participating institutions categorize their data into three types: trusted for reliable tasks, counterfactual for training models, and counterexample for identifying and rectifying data flaws. Following initial model training at individual sites, the FSI framework ensures that: (1) only trusted data is used for subsequent tasks, (2) a subset of participating sites contribute their counterfactual data to train a centralized model, and (3) sites that provided counterexample data are given priority for further data contribution. Moreover, the proposed approach incorporates counterfactual reinforcement learning to incentivize sites to contribute high-quality data, while minimizing cheating behavior. Experimental evaluations conducted on simulated and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the FSI framework in improving model performance, reducing data heterogeneity, and combating cheeseaking behavior. Furthermore, a feasibility study on healthcare datasets highlights the practical applications of FSI in healthcare. The proposed framework is scalable, adaptable, and secure, making it suitable for large-scale healthcare settings. The code for the proposed approach is available at https://github.com/lingeyu/FederatedSelectiveIntegration.

Re-examining the tau lepton's form factor, specifically its electric dipole moment, is crucial for maintaining consistency with the anomalous magnetic moment of the electron. To calculate this form factor, we employ a range of approaches, including perturbative QCD, perturbative QCD with residual effects, and also rely on input from experimental measurements, particularly the tau's decay patterns. Nevertheless, the magnitude of the tau's electric dipole remains uncertain, with estimates ranging broadly from $10.41 \times 10^{-18}$ e cm to $10.69 \times 10^{-18}$ e cm, and even further to $10.7 \times 10^{-18}$ e cm in some models. Consequently, determining this form factor with higher precision is essential for identifying potential connections between physics at the TeV scale and low-energy phenomena. Additionally, we explore the implications of a larger tau electric dipole for neutrino properties, specifically whether it could indicate the existence of additional light states beyond the Standard Model. To this end, we find that combining the electron's and tau's anomalous magnetic moments with a range of assumptions regarding the number of light degrees of freedom above 4.2 GeV results in a novel bound on the absolute value of the tau's electric dipole moment: $|d_\tau| < 1.66 \times 10^{-18}$ e cm. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this bound bridges the gap between the approach of treating the tau's electric dipole as a contact interaction and the approach that considers it as a form factor, and that it holds in the limit where the number of light degrees of freedom is negligible. We obtained high-cadence photometric and spectroscopic data for SN~2020jfo in various wavelengths, covering the spectrum from U to K bands. This Type II supernova exhibited an unusually brief plateau phase, lasting only 20 days, which is the shortest known to date. By analyzing H-alpha emission profiles, we found that the initial expansion velocities of the ejections were higher than typical Type II supernovae. Additionally, SN~2020jfo demonstrated a more notable presence of [Fe III] and weaker H recombination than usual, indicating a shorter photosphere temperature decline rate. Using the $E_p-\text{extent of} [Fe III]/H$ ratio and the $V-band$ plateau duration models, we determined that SN~2020jfo was an 10±2 Peaked Energy explosive event of Type II. Furthermore, we found that the 64.63±13.51 day $\gamma$-ray prompt collapse period was significantly shorter than the 22.57±4.08 day primary rise phase, indicating that the prompt collapse period is dependent on the primary rise phase rather than the explosive energy. This finding challenges the current understanding that primary rise phases are independent of the explosive energy. Lastly, SN~2020jfo showed a 12.57±2.08 mag absolute peak magnitude, which is more luminous than typical Type II supernovae. This, along with the extremely brief plateau phase, the faster expansion velocity, the unique spectroscopic characteristics, and the particular ejection composition, makes SN~2020jfo an exceptional supernova that fits into a specific category of Type II supernovae named IIps. To greatly decrease the number of image sensors required in wide-field X-ray monitors employing lobster-eye lenses, we propose a concept where multiple lobster-eye lenses are combined to cover a single field of view. Each lens is attached to a separate image sensor, and these sensors are then combined to create a single, more comprehensive image of the field of view. By minimizing the number of image sensors, their total cost can be significantly reduced, in addition to lowering power consumption and increasing durability. Furthermore, a smaller number of image sensors results in a shorter time it takes to read out the image, allowing for faster monitoring of transient X-ray events. We demonstrate this concept using a simulation where a single lobster-eye lens with a 4 square degree field of view is combined with 16 small image sensors, each with a 1 square degree field of view, completely covering a 16 square degree field of view. We show that the point spread function (PSF) of the array is similar to the PSF of a single lobster-eye lens, and that the contrast ratio of the array to a single lobster-eye lens is nearly indistinguishable. We also examine various configurations of the multi-lens array and discuss possible applications in transient X-ray science. Although this concept is particularly suitable for monitors employing lobster-eye lenses, it can be adapted to other types of X-ray optics. We suggest the name "Muller array" for this concept, named after the German word "Mullerauge", literally "eye of the mole". The Muller array can be configured to optimize for a range of fields of view, and we provide a straightforward method for calculating the ideal number of lenses and their spacing to achieve a desired field of view. We also examine the effects of the size of the image sensors, the spacing of the lenses, the number of lenses, and the size of the field of view on the cost, power consumption, durability, and performance of the array. We conclude by discussing possible implementations and the results of a cost estimate for a Muller array designed to monitor a specific field of view. To address this issue, an effective method has been developed to detect and identify misleading news using a combination of linguistic and technical approaches. To further enhance the method's efficacy, it has been combined with a learning-based approach to deal with ambiguous information, which has been empirically proven to significantly improve the method's performance in detecting challenging cases. The proposed technique has been thoroughly tested and its performance evaluated against existing methods using a vast dataset of 50,000 news articles, which yields a 97% accuracy rate in detecting false news articles.
