We present DynaSOAr, a parallel memory allocator tailored for object-oriented programming on GPUs. By introducing a novel "allocation region" concept, DynaSOAr separates memory spaces for base classes and derived classes, enabling efficient multiple-inheritance and performance gains. Although targeting high-performance computing applications, the allocator's simplicity and object-oriented features also make it suitable for a range of other parallel object-oriented developments. We have tested DynaSOAr across a range of benchmarks and applications, including a popular physics simulation framework, and found its memory usage and execution speed to outperform a naive approach using raw pointers. Further, we show that DynaSOAr yields significant performance benefits when utilizing a GPU's fast register memory. The full allocator source code is available openly for public use.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model, applicable to all impurity states, incorporates the effects of hybridization, magnetic moment, and orbital motion. It yields expressions for the energies and widths of the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states, particularly the central and asymmetric states that form in the gap of a superconductor due to the interaction between a magnetic impurity and the surrounding electrons. This framework has been utilized to investigate the YSR states generated by Manganese impurities on the Nb(110) surface, comparing the results to experimental data obtained using angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy. The simulation reproduces the known behavior of YSR states and predicts additional features associated with combined states, revealing their dependence on the orientation of the magnetic moment and the absence of combined states within the energy gap of the superconductor. Additionally, it is demonstrated that the YSR states formed by a single impurity and a dimer located close to each other exhibit distinct combined states that evolve as the distance between the impurities changes, altering the symmetry of the states and causing them to move across the energy gap of the superconductor. This theoretical analysis agrees with experimental findings and provides a comprehensive understanding of the YSR states and their combined effects in a superconductor, giving insight into the interplay between electron pairing, magnetic moments, and the local symmetry of the impurity states. This understanding can be applied to a wide range of magnetic impurities on a superconducting surface. The code used for this simulation can be accessed at https://git.io/AMScode. We investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO2.  To analyze these properties, we used a 48-atom supercell via the VASP code, considering 2x2x1 duplication of the crystal structure.  For N dopants, our findings showed that n-type magnetic behavior could be achieved with an electron configuration of [Sc 3d^1 4d^1], and that this result is dependent on the position of the N atoms within the supercell, as well as the level of U correlation correction.  In contrast, C dopants resulted in non-magnetic behavior, with a [Sc 3d^0 4d^0] electron configuration.  To reduce computational costs, we repeated the calculations using a 2x2x2 supercell, with results indicating that the C dopant exhibits non-magnetic behavior in smaller electron configurations, with [Sc 3d^0 4d^0], and that the N dopant shows magnetic behavior in larger electron configurations, with [Sc 3d^1 4d^1].  We also explored the effects of different dopant locations and lattice parameters on the Wigner-Seitz radius.  Our study indicated that N dopants at the Ti site result in the largest Wigner-Seitz radius, while C and N dopants at the O site, as well as N dopants at the interstitial site, exhibit similar, smaller Wigner-Seitz radii.  We concluded that N dopants at the Ti site may exhibit both magnetic behavior and large Wigner-Seitz radius, making them suitable for enhancing both magnetism and photocatalytic activity in TiO2.  We recommend experimenting with N dopants at the Ti site via both theoretical and experimental methods.  We also suggested possible pathways for achieving this arrangement, including particle irradiation and chemical treatment. Consequently, extending the search for elastic top production to include vector boson pairs will provide valuable insights into this phenomenon and facilitate a more comprehensive understanding of the underlying physics. To achieve this, we propose analyzing datasets from forward proton-scattering experiments at the Large Hadron Collider, specifically looking for high-mass vector boson pairs produced through an elastic process. To this end, we outline a strategy for utilizing zero-bias missing-proton triggers, identify potential kinematic regions of interest, and provide estimates for detecting elastic top and vector boson pair production. Additionally, we outline alternatives for triggering on forward jets and protons, as well as methods for interpreting findings in the context of production processes. Given the limited amount of existing data and without any optimization, we demonstrate that the large majority of existing elastic top production signals can be recovered, and that the number of expected events exceeds the number of background events by a factor of ten. The non-relativistic, massless QED model known as scalar Quantum Electrodynamics (sQED) exhibits a highly interesting phase structure consisting of a confining phase and a conformal phase, separated by a sharp crossovers at a critical number of fermion flavors. Since the conformal phase is inaccessible to direct computation owing to the model's analytic inaccuracy, its properties must be inferred indirectly. Quantum simulations employing cavity QED systems can provide an alternative route to examining the conformal phase, although the limited number fidelity of qudit preparation poses a constraint. This study utilizes qudits instead of qubits to overcome this fidelity issue, assessing various sound propagation properties in the conformal phase to verify the consistency of simulation results. Additionally, qudit quantization regulations are investigated to ensure the accessibility of simulation data. A comment on the relation between sound propagation speeds and the Wightman function is also made, as well as a discussion on the detectability of the conformal phase transition and the relevance of qudit fidelity to this goal. A proposed qudit duality technique is introduced to explore this issue further. Lastly, the potential of a specific, highly available qudit state preparation protocol is examined. This protocol, based on a combined Gray code, enables efficient simulation of double-well potentials in quantum simulations of sQED. This code has been tested extensively to validate its correctness and efficiency, and its applicability has been demonstrated to double-well potential simulations, a model renowned for its intricate phase structure. This research investigates the concept of a group with a finite diameter relative to its underlying field, which is a fundamental idea originally developed for associative algebras by their non-degenerate representations. We examine the case where the diameter is set to a finite number, then translate this condition into a polynomial constraint. This leads to a characterization of the group's structure, revealing it is composed of a direct product of cyclic groups and an associative matrix algebra defined over a finite field. Additionally, we establish a related criterion for the group's unity property, i.e. its ability to operate as a universal multilinear polynomial operator. Further, we provide a specific formula for any universal polynomial operator associated with this group. Lastly, we conclude by exploring specific examples of these groups, both finite and infinite. Semicisely, we analyze the particular instance of a group defined by the set of its elements, the operation of adding those elements modulo a finite integer, and the field of its complex numbers. This includes determining the specific diameter of that particular group, as well as the number of its non-degenerate representation types, the number of its prime factorization types, the number of its distinct universal multilinear polynomial operators, and the length of its shortest universal multilinear polynomial operators. Moreover, we establish an applicable theorem for any group with a finite diameter, demonstrating its capacity to be expressed as a finite algebraic expression, as well as providing a related criterion for its unity property, and finally determining the specific diameter, number of non-degenerate representation types, number of prime factorization types, number of universal multilinear polynomial operators, and the length of its shortest universal multilinear polynomial operators. This research was originally published in the journal Advances in Mathematics Volume 383, 2021, Article number 107965.

A statistical approach to analyzing the spectral energy distributions of young massive infrared dark clouds has indicated that the massic core function, a key component in the radiative transfer models, is often missing in areas with significant star formation. However, our research found a pattern of core development in the Dragon infrared dark nebula, where the massic core function is present and the underlying radiative transfer models suggest a higher fraction of gas associated with the core than typically found in similar regions. We interpret this as evidence of core development and progressing collapse, and believe it is a prerequisite for massive star formation to occur. Nevertheless, we also found a smaller subset of areas with low core mass function values, and we propose these may be affected by external factors influencing the molecular gas distribution. Despite these findings, we conclude that the majority of the Dragon nebula is progressing towards collapse and likely star formation, with a possible variation in core development levels across its different segments. The absence of core mass function components and the presence of HII regions in a small portion of the Dragon nebula do however complicate this picture. The research was carried out as part of the GASTRO-COLLAB project, and the results were obtained using the RADMOD and MODFIND tools on SFDC and IRAC data. The core development in the Dragon nebula has significant implications for the massive infrared dark galaxy array, and similar patterns of core development are likely present in other regions with similar characteristics. The statistical analysis of the data also yielded a marked concentration of massic core function components in the center of the Dragon nebula, which we believe is influenced by its orientation with respect to the surrounding environment. We observed the flow of liquid foams on surfaces with different textures, including regularly spaced pillars and layered textures. Interestingly, our findings show that layered textures can allow the flow to resume even after it has slowed or stuck, due to the occurrence of local stick-slip phenomena that happen in the gaps between the pillars. However, the safety of these processes can depend on the depth of the texture, especially when it exceeds half the size of the space between the pillars. Our further experiments modify the texture's geometry to accelerate the flow's resumption, achieving this effect by creating the texture's geometry on an angle. Our research provides practical information for optimizing textures that can prevent the stick-slip phenomenon and safe operation of fluid flow processes. This was accomplished by systematically varying the rate of wall rotation and slowing down the interface's speed. The resulting patterns show a smooth interface breaking into a series of curved rosettes as the wall rotation speed increases. A balance between the stress imposed by the curved interface and the centrifugal force generated by the wall rotation speeds remains evident across different rates of wall rotation. This stress balance allows for the inclusion of a correction that seamlessly connects the results to earlier experiments on spinning Hele-Shaw cells with fixed interfaces. Furthermore, a transition from sharp-edged finger tips to a more rounded shape occurs as the rate of wall rotation increases, which can be understood by considering the effects of wall curvature on a single finger. The interface's stability was influenced by the rate of wall rotation, but this effect became less noticeable as the interface became turbulent. A possible explanation for this phenomenon is that the interface's interaction with the rotating wall causes it to become unstable at a lower speed than it would in a stationary Hele-Shaw cell. The results presented here remain valid across a range of speeds and wall rotation rates, as the geometry and dynamics of the interface can be characterized by a single, non-dimensional curve that remains unchanged even when the interface's speed or the rate of wall rotation change. This is demonstrated by varying the rate of wall rotation from 0 to 13 times the rate of interface advancement, and the speed of the interface from 1 to 100 times the rate of wall rotation. The behavior of a advancing interface in a Hele-Shaw cell with rotating side walls has some relevance to the dynamics of a interface in a rotating fluid, but it differs from that situation because the interface in the Hele-Shaw cell is constrained to move in a horizontal plane by its own buoyancy. The significant discrepancy between advancing computational technology and pace of tangible applications sparked the concept of a "translation gap." To bridge this gap, the term "translation" became a core objective for various scientific fields. This paper explores an unpublished yet seminal work by the author, a framework for adapting grid computing to various settings, which we will refer to as the DC4Framework. This framework successfully facilitated the development of a grid computing system for a peer-to-peer video transmission application among university students. In contrast to other research on grid computing, this work focuses on a real-world scenario rather than purely theoretical aspects. However, due limitations, the DC4Framework remained an unfinished project. Nonetheless, its components demonstrate a tangible translation process. Building upon the DC4Framework, we developed a more comprehensive grid computing system called the DC4Toolchain. In this paper, we outline the DC4Toolchain, highlighting how it addresses issues with the original DC4Framework and providing an overall toolchain structure. Furthermore, we outline a methodology for evaluating the performance of the DC4Toolchain, which could be adapted for assessing other grid applications. Leveraging the DC4Toolchain, we implemented and evaluated a grid computing system for video transmission among university students. The resulting system outperformed a non-distributed approach by reducing encoding time by approximately 62% and transmission time by approximately 77%. We also tested the robustness of the DC4Toolchain and found it capable of adapting to dynamic environments with some limitations. Ultimately, this research provides an actionable guide for developing grid computing systems, as well as a usable toolchain for evaluating the performance of such systems. The underlying principles of the DC4Toolchain are versatile and could be applied to other grid applications, whereas the specific implementation of the P2P video transmission system is particular to the particular challenge it addresses. This theory predicts that a $J/\psi$ decay into a photon and invisible matter might occur, with a predicted probability of $1.5 \times 10^{-5}$. This work introduces a new method, singular spectrum examination (SSE), for analyzing multivariate functional time series data across different dimensional spaces. Building on the singular spectrum analysis (SSA) technique, SSE identifies prominent patterns within these data sets by constructing a set of multivariate functional eigenvectors through an optimization process. A key feature of this method is its ability to handle multivariate data across distinct dimensional spaces, making SSE applicable to a broad range of scenarios. Furthermore, SSE is actionable for forecasters and researchers as the technique provides a clear, interpretable understanding of complex data by highlighting significant features and allowing for space-based analysis. We demonstrate the effectiveness of SSE with simulations and real-world data, including a analysis of multivariate functional time series in the context of nonlinear dynamics. The technique is also compared to multivariate functional principal component analysis (MFPCA), a more computationally intensive but related method, and multivariate vector autoregression (MVAR), a more computationally lightweight but less informative method, to validate its performance. The results show that SSE outperforms MFPCA and MVAR in terms of reconstruction accuracy and model selection criteria such as the Akaike information criterion (AIC) and the Bayesian information criterion (BIC). Finally, we apply SSE to a multivariate functional time series model consisting of three dimensional spaces to derive predictive models and to analyze a dataset of spatial temperature patterns across Canada. The code for SSE is publicly available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/abdo22/SingSpectEx. The results presented in this paper were obtained using R version 4.1.2 and the suggested package rssa version 2.4. While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively training such models is complicated due to issues such as nuclei that are fused with each other, or with the surrounding tissue background. To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods of automatic nucleus segmentation based on point annotation, which has yielded notable improvements in model performance. However, these methods require the manual annotation of images by experienced pathologists, thus increasing the workload. To make cancer diagnosis more efficient, it's crucial to develop a fully automatic nucleus segmentation algorithm capable of accurately locating and extracting valuable information from images with minimal manual intervention. Lastly, a comparative analysis is presented between the proposed model and existing Bass, ATter, and LinkNet based models, highlighting the W-Net's superior performance. In a gravity theory, a scalar field is generated through a Chern-Simons form, which involves a gauge field, and this formulation has been successfully applied to describe the characteristics of rotating black holes in certain contexts. This paper investigates the fundamentals of an alternative gravity theory that is based on a scalar field and gauge forces, and it provides a comprehensive review of explicit solutions, including black holes and solitons that rotate and have hairy characteristics. A unique set of Einstein-Dirac-Scalar equations has been derived for this specific gravity theory, and it can be solved for a range of scenarios, such as: static solitons with zero charge or spin; solitons that rotate without charge; black holes that rotate without charge; and black holes that rotate with charge. This paper also examines the boundaries between which types of solutions exist, and it highlights the unique features of each solution. A comprehensive appendix has been included to demonstrate how the original Chern-Simons form can be re-expressed for complex gauge forces, and it provides an alternative formulation of the Einstein-Dirac-Scalar equations. A further subsection of the appendix is also given to describe a complex self-dual gauge force, and it discusses the implications of this context for the soliton solutions. A comprehensive set of metrics, scalar field profiles, and energy distributions has been presented for each solution type, and it provides a clear understanding of the properties of each solution. A discussion on the energy spectra and angular momenta of the static solitons, as well as the counter-part discussion on the black holes, has been included in the paper. A comparison has been made between the results of this specific gravity theory and the corresponding results of the Einstein gravity theory, and it has been found that the results of the Einstein gravity theory can be recovered when the Chern-Simons term is set to zero. A commentary has been provided on how this specific gravity theory relates to the conformal gravity theory, and it has been found that the results of the conformal gravity theory can be recovered when the Chern-Simons term is set to zero and the metric multiplet interacts with a complex self-dual gauge field in a specific context known as the Bagger-Wise model. global considerations. Yet, the fundamental question of how hierarchical 
structures emerge in games involving multiple levels of interaction has rarely 
been explored. This study investigates a stochastic pursuit-evasion game on a 
grid, where agents at different spatial scales competitively pursue or evade 
each other. Our findings reveal that hierarchical divisions can reduce the 
prevalence of evasion and increase the probability of pursuit succeeding. We 
show that the most efficient hierarchical parities are those that prioritize the 
protection of internal areas over the control of external borders. Furthermore, 
these HIERARCHIES exhibit a unique property: they divide the grid into distinct 
regions, each behaving as independent purification agents in a stochastic process. The development of these hierarchical structures is a natural consequence of the balance between local interactions and the need for scalability, and it has implications for the study and optimization of complex networks, allowing for the improvement of strategies in a wide range of games, including routing, voting, and navigation scenarios. The integration of local and global considerations presented here can also be applied to the study and optimization of other spatial phenomena, including the development of sustainable urban environments, the optimization of supply chains, and the analysis of voting patterns in geographic regions. Due to the advancing capabilities and fast nature of proton-proton collisions, the role of muon colliders has evolved significantly, shifting from a focus on top quark pair production to a broader range of processes, including vector boson pair production, scalar mass determination, and top quark effective field theories. To take advantage of this change, it's essential to have highly efficient methods for estimating vector boson properties, such as the mass of the weak force carriers W and Z. In this paper, we present multiple approaches to accurately determine the mass of these particles in muon colliders, and compare the performance of these methods to the traditional use of kinematic distributions in proton-proton colliders. We also explore the potential of these methods at two specific types of muon colliders: incident-only and merging modes. In incident-only mode, where incoming muons collide with each other, we find that the most accurate methods involve reconstructing the decay angles of the vector bosons, particularly in pairs, and combining this information with the transverse momenta of the particles. This results in masses estimated from collisions to be within 0.1 GeV of the true mass, for both W and Z bosons. In contrast, at incident-only mode, the most efficient methods involve estimating the mass based on the distribution of the sum of the masses of the outgoing particles, which still achieves a 0.5 GeV level of accuracy. In merging mode, where incoming muons are combined with additional particles before colliding with each other, we find that the most accurate methods involve reconstructing the full four-momentum of the vector bosons, which achieves a level of mass estimation within 0.05 GeV of the true mass. We also explore the applications of these methods to specific processes, such as pair production of vector bosons, as well as the combination of these methods with the use of kinematic distributions used in proton-proton colliders. We conclude that muon colliders offer vast opportunities for discovering and determining the properties of vector boson pair production, and that this can be achieved through the development of efficient methods for estimating the mass of these particles. We hope that this work will contribute to the advancement of this field, and provide a starting point for further investigations into the dynamics of these processes. We also outline potential directions for such investigations, including the study of effective field theories, scalar mass determination, and the development of event generators. We introduce a novel model where five specific types of digital trees gather under the direction of their individual natural numerals. Initially, each tree resides in a designated sector of a limitless, one-dimensional plane defined by the set of natural numbers. The plane's evolution is determined by simple rules: each tree moves horizontally or remains stationary based on a specific comparison with the numeral indicated at its leftmost edge; in response to this comparison, the tree then extends its edge horizontally or remains fixed. The rule that governs the tree's movement is aligned with the principles of intuitionistic logic. We prove that in this model, the trees that start in the leftmost sector will gather on the right, the trees in the sector numbered three will gather on the left, and the trees in the middle sector will disperse. Additionally, we provide explicit numerical boundaries for the gathering of the rightmost sector, the distance between the leading and trailing edges of the middle sector, and the location of the leading edge of the leftmost sector. In the process of our analysis, we introduce a new, intuitive metric that allows these conclusions to be drawn. Furthermore, we show that the rules governing the movement of the trees are equivalent to the application of the fixed point theorem as described by the Curry scheme, and that this situation can be extended to the movement of multiple trees. Lastly, we provide a precise numerical value for the distance between the leading and trailing edges of the leftmost sector, and offer a simpler, intuitive explanation for the behavior of the trees in this model. In the process of our analysis, we make use of a novel interpretation of the Godel operator that is motivated by the context of this model. This interpretation leads to the derivation of the Curry scheme by way of the fixed point theorem, and provides a reason for which intuitionistic logic is more conducive to gathering behavior than classical logic. In the course of our discussion, we also make reference to the original work of Godel, Tarski, Carnap, and Rosser, and offer a specific numerical value for the sum of the distances between the leading and trailing edges of the trees in the rightmost and leftmost sectors. Furthermore, we provide a general formula for the sum of the distances between the leading and trailing edges of the trees in any given sector, and offer a separate, independent proof for this formula based on the principles of classical logic. This latter proof leads to a different numerical value for the sum of the distances between the leading and trailing edges of the trees in the rightmost and leftmost sectors

This paper formulates the three spheres theorem for non-negative Clifford analytic functions associated with a specific parameter, and also investigates the scenario for functions associated with no particular parameter. Additionally, three spheres theorems are established for harmonic functions in three-dimensional space. A comprehensive discussion on theorems and their applications is provided in the paper, including cases with zero-order and first-order Riemannian Laplacians. A notable connection with the classical three spheres theorem for harmonic functions is demonstrated. A comprehensive analysis of previously known results and theorems from notable researchers such as H. Leitner, G. Price, and V. M. Tortso, is also presented in the paper. A three spheres theorem for a non-negative harmonic function $u$ is given by the paper, which implies that $u$ can be expressed as a sum of the mean value of $u$ over three spheres and a function that is identically zero in the interior of the smallest sphere. This result can be generalized to harmonic functions in a space of $n$ dimensions. A notable connection between the three spheres theorems for harmonic functions and the Dirac operator is demonstrated in the paper. A three spheres theorem for the Dirac operator $D_m$ is given by the paper, which implies that a harmonic function $u$ can be expressed as a sum of the mean value of $u$ over three spheres and a function that is identically zero in the interior of the smallest sphere, for the space of harmonic functions in a space of $m$ dimensions with the metric defined by the operator $D_m$. A three spheres theorem for the Riemannian Laplacian $\Delta$ is given by the paper, which implies that a harmonic function $u$ can be expressed as a sum of the mean value of $u$ over three spheres and a function that is identically zero in the interior of the smallest sphere, for the space of harmonic functions in a space of $m$ dimensions with the metric defined by the operator $\Delta$. A comprehensive discussion on the results from the three spheres theorems for harmonic functions, the Riemannian Laplacian $\Delta$, the Dirac operator $D_m$, and the monogenic functions associated with the parameter $\lambda$ is presented in the paper. Recently, machine learning techniques have encountered challenges related to data inverses, which arise when training models with data that includes sensitive information that should be removed. Posterior extraction, a related task, involves using trained models to generate sensitive information from non-sensitive data, without accessing the original data used for training. In this work, we focus on the problem of posterior extraction from trained natural language processing models, without access to the original labeled data. We develop a novel method, a regularized conditional GAN called rg-CGAN, that efficiently recovers the posterior by combining a conditional GAN with regularization techniques. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by applying it to inverse issues related to sensitive text categories. Our method achieves superior performance compared to alternative methods in three different settings: recursive extraction, partial extraction, and binary extraction. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghrua/rg-CGAN.

Recently, significant advancements in graph neural networks (GNNs) have been driven by large-scale dataset training, thanks to the development of scalable and efficient GNN models such as LightGCN and AttEnt. However, these improvements rely on the assumption that similar objects have similar labels, which is not universally applicable. In fact, many real-world tasks involve distinguishing between categories of vastly different natures, such as separating objects from backgrounds in image recognition. To address this issue, we propose a novel GNN framework called Lorentzian GNN (LGNN), which introduces a layer that compares node representations using the Lorentzian metric, resulting in a contrastive loss that contrasts similar node pairs. By adjusting the hyperparameter of the Lorentzian decay factor, LGNN can effectively handle tasks with large category gaps. To further improve performance, we derive an expression for the gradient of the Lorentzian GNN layer and apply an adaptive update rule to enhance the effectiveness of random walk. In experiments on datasets with large category gaps, LGNN achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art baselines, and we demonstrate the scalability and flexibility of LGNN by conducting ablation studies and analyzing the impact of hyperparameters. Moreover, LGNN exceeds baseline performance on standard classification and recommendation tasks. To facilitate widespread adoption, we open-source LGNN at https://github.com/zwang84/LGNN.

This model's parameter, $\alpha$, plays a significant role in determining decision-making behaviors under uncertainty, and we found that students who excel in mathematics tend to have different $\alpha$ values compared to those who are struggling in mathematics. Furthermore, we observed that the Tsallis-like model's $\alpha$ value is linked to the frame switching theory, particularly in regards to the exponential delay discounting parameter $k$. However, we also found that the model's $\alpha$ value is influenced by uncertainty, which in turn affects decision-making behaviors. Additionally, we found that the Tsallis-like model's $\alpha$ value is associated with the degree of diversity or complexity in decision-making, which is supported by Tsallis statistics. These findings suggest that optimal decision-making arises from a state of "golden ratio" balance between the exclusion of redundant information and the maintenance of complex diversity. Therefore, we propose that the Tsallis-like delay discounting model can be utilized as a tool for evaluating an individual's ability to handle uncertainty and their cognitive complexity. Lastly, we proposed that the model's $\alpha$ value can be utilized to differentiate between individuals who exhibit rigid thinking patterns and those who demonstrate cognitive flexibility. In conclusion, we demonstrated that the Tsallis-like delay discounting model provides novel insights into decision-making behaviors under uncertainty, and it offers a precise metric for evaluating an individual's cognitive complexity, which can be utilized in various applications across psychology, economics, and sports. We introduce a new paradigm, the "most basic scoto-seesaw framework", which applies universal principles to reconcile the incompatibility between dark matter masslessness and the stability of the vacuum within the Standard Model. This framework incorporates a single complex spherical vector operator, allowing for both scalar and vector dark matter particles. The "phenomenological sector" of the framework consists of an $SU(2)_L$ singlet scalar and a pair of complex singlet scalar fields connected by a dark sector coupling. We examine the implications of this setup for Weak Interaction Relativity and find that it is consistent with dark matter data, although it predicts a dark matter mass above a few GeV. Furthermore, the vacuum stability and electroweak symmetry breaking conditions define a triadic relationship among the dark sector coupling, the vacuum stability scale, and the electroweak scale. We determine the region of parameter space that meets these conditions and demonstrate that the setup maintains stability in high energy regimes. Additionally, we determine the cross-section for dark matter particle interactions and verify that the setup complies with experimental constraints. We also explore the possibility of neutrino mass generation within this framework and find that it requires additional fields. Nevertheless, we demonstrate that the setup can be modified to accommodate neutrino mass. We conclude that the most basic scoto-seesaw framework provides a versatile and comprehensive description of dark matter and the vacuum stability problem. We anticipate that this setup will serve as a valuable foundation for analyzing more complex versions of the scoto-seesaw framework and for exploring the relationship between vacuum stability and dark sector couplings in various dark matter scenarios. We investigate relative quantum topological invariants for algebraic varieties, building on the principles of mixed Hodge theory and the Birch and Swinnerton-Polya Conjecture. Specifically, we explore how these invariants respond to certain changes, particularly those that alter the geometric part of a relative pair (V/K, Sh). These changes include switching from a variety defined over a global field of characteristic zero to its twisted form, as well as changing the embedding of a variety within a projective space. We also examine the behavior of these invariants when the variety in question is modified through a purely birational alteration, without any change to its absolute or relative invariants. Finally, we establish that two varieties have identical absolute or relative invariants if and only if they are directly related to each other, provided this condition holds for all subfields of the original field. This is equivalent to the statement that two varieties have the same invariants if and only if they can be converted from one form to the other through a series of specific algebraic transformations. We further show that a particular combination of Euler numbers and a product of L-functions serves as a complete and comprehensive set of absolute invariants for a variety, provided this set is defined with respect to the variety's own perspective. We also demonstrate that the invariants of a variety remain unchanged even when the variety itself is altered through a process called monodromy transformation. We further investigate the relationship between the invariants of a variety and the coefficients of its Hasse-Weil L-function, specifically the case of hyperelliptic curves, specific types of K3 surfaces, and a particular class of Calabi-Yau hypersurfaces. The safety of radiology technicians relies on proper infection control measures to prevent the spread of infectious diseases. To facilitate training and evaluation for these technicians, simulated images with intentional markings can be used in a classroom setting. Currently, available resources, primarily generated by computers, do not account for the specific markings left behind when technicians incorrectly use certain equipment. This study aims to address this limitation by collecting real images with the actual markings left by an ultrasound probe on patients' chests, which can also be annotated for machine learning applications. A publicly available dataset consisting of 180 images with 35 different markings is presented, along with a method for automatically identifying these markings. This research can be used for training machines to detect the markings, enabling the synthetic generation of images with similar markings, or it can be directly utilized by training machines to predict the presence of specific markings on new images, which can further lead to insights on areas frequently affected by infections. To demonstrate the potential of this dataset for machine learning, a basic classification model was trained to detect the presence of a particular marking, resulting in an accuracy of over 90%. This study offers various machine learning models suitable for incorporating into future applications, including an operator warning system that could alert technicians about the spread of diseases based on the markings left on patients. This dataset, available for public use, is named CXRProbes and can be accessed through a dedicated website. This research paves the way for safer working conditions and the development of intelligent warning systems for radiology technicians. This work is particularly relevant for detecting and correcting proper ultrasound probe technique, as shown in a related study, but its applications extend to other fields involving patient interaction, such as electrocardiography and endoscopy.
